t.the airavatesvara temple complex@10.9,79:
Darasuram is a quiet town in the Kaveri delta, a few kilometres from Kumbakonam, and its temple is one of the gems of Chola architecture. The Airavatesvara temple was built in the twelfth century under Rajaraja II, and it is smaller and more delicate than the great temple of Thanjavur, as though the Cholas, at the height of their power, had decided to put their energy into detail. Every surface is carved: miniature friezes of dancers and musicians, the stories of the Shaiva saints, and narrow panels of gods and animals in fine, polished stone.

The temple's mandapa is built as a stone chariot, with huge carved wheels and horses, and the stairs of one of its platforms are said to produce musical notes when tapped. Legend says that Airavata, the white elephant of the king of the gods, worshipped here to be cured of a curse, which gives the shrine its name. Together with the Brihadisvara temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram, it is listed as one of the Great Living Chola Temples, living because worship goes on every day.

The ride here is flat and green. The Kaveri delta is one of the most fertile parts of southern India, a landscape of rice paddies, coconut palms, banana groves and irrigation canals, and the roads run straight between them, lined with trees and dotted with temple towers. Roads are generally decent but busy with trucks, buses, bullock carts and motorbikes, and the usual rules apply: stay alert, expect cattle and sudden stops, and avoid night riding. Heat is a given; the cooler months from November to February are far more comfortable, and the monsoon between October and December brings heavy rain.

Swamimalai is a few kilometres away and known for its bronze casting, and Kumbakonam, a bigger town just beyond, has fuel, food and many temples. Remove shoes before entering the temple, and expect the stone floor to be hot at midday. Early light is best, and filter coffee in a small restaurant afterwards is a pleasure.
t.nako@31.9,78.6:
Nako is a village you reach after a day of mountain road, and you feel the effort as soon as you arrive. It lies at about 3,600 metres in the Hangrang valley of Kinnaur, in Himachal Pradesh, close to the border with Tibet. The village is built of stone and timber and clings to a hillside above a small lake, with willow and poplar trees around its edge and the great peak of Reo Purgyil standing in the distance, more than 6,700 metres high.

Culturally you have crossed a line here. Kinnaur is a mix of Hindu and Buddhist traditions, and Nako has a group of old Buddhist temples dating back, according to tradition, to the time of the translator Rinchen Zangpo, who spread Buddhism in the western Himalaya about a thousand years ago. Inside are wall paintings and clay statues that have survived the cold and the centuries. The lake freezes in winter and in summer reflects the sky.

The riding is the real adventure. The road follows the Sutlej and Spiti rivers through steep gorges, and in places it is cut into the rock above a drop of hundreds of metres, with narrow sections, rockfall and landslides. Hairpins climb to the village from the valley floor. Expect gravel patches, water crossings after rain and sudden changes in weather. Altitude is serious, so acclimatise before you push on, and watch for signs of mountain sickness. The best season is from late spring to early autumn, because snow closes the road in winter.

Reckong Peo, further down the valley, and Kaza in Spiti are the larger centres, and both have fuel pumps, though supplies can run short. Small guesthouses and cafes offer simple food, usually dal, rice, momos and tea. Regulations for foreigners and permits in border areas change, so check with local authorities before you go. The reward is the lake at dawn, with smoke from the kitchen fires rising into clear, cold air.
t.shimla@31.1,77.2:
Shimla is where the British came to escape the heat of the plains, and it still has the look of a Surrey town that took a wrong turn into the Himalaya. Built along a ridge at roughly twenty-two hundred metres, with pine and cedar trees and rows of red-roofed houses, it served as the summer capital of British India, and decisions affecting hundreds of millions of people were made here between May and October. The Ridge, an open promenade in the centre, is lined with Christ Church, a pale yellow neo-Gothic building of the 1850s, and the Mall, a long shopping street, runs alongside. Vehicles are restricted on the Mall and the Ridge, so you will park below and walk up.

Above town, Jakhu hill carries a temple to the monkey god Hanuman and the monkeys that go with it, who are known to snatch glasses, snacks and anything that is not fastened down. Keep your gloves and food in the top box. Out of town, the Viceregal Lodge, a grey stone mansion in the Elizabethan style, now houses a research institute and is open for visits. The narrow-gauge railway from Kalka, ninety-six kilometres of curves, tunnels and viaducts, is listed by UNESCO and is a lovely way to arrive if you have no bike.

For riders, this is the start of the Spiti circuit and a place to prepare. The road east, the old Hindustan-Tibet road, follows the Sutlej river through Narkanda, Rampur and the apple country of Kinnaur, climbing steadily into a world of steeper valleys, thinner air and bigger mountains. Traffic leaving Shimla is thick and slow, with buses, trucks and taxis grinding along the narrow road, and in the monsoon, from July to September, landslides can block it for hours or days. Check the road status each morning.

Shimla has more than a hundred and seventy thousand people, and fuel and repair shops are no problem. Stock up on spares, cash and warm clothing here, because supplies thin out quickly after Reckong Peo. The best times to ride are May to June and September to October, when the sky is clear and the passes are open.

The town is at its best in the early morning, when mist rises from the valleys and the first light touches the snow peaks far to the north.
t.kaza@32.2,78.1:
Spiti means the middle land, the place between India and Tibet, and Kaza is its capital in the way that a cluster of low whitewashed buildings in a very large landscape can be a capital. It lies at about thirty-eight hundred metres on the bank of the Spiti river, in a wide valley of grey and ochre mountains with almost no trees, where the sky is a hard dark blue and the air is thin and dry. The climate is cold desert, with snow in winter and little rain in summer, and the people live by barley, peas and yak herding, and by the monasteries that have shaped life here for a thousand years.

Key monastery, a Tibetan Buddhist complex stacked up a hilltop a short way from town, is the one to see, and the village of Kibber, higher still, has a claim to be among the highest inhabited places in the world connected by road. Langza, with its fossils from an ancient sea bed, and Hikkim, with a post office that claims to be the highest in the world, lie in the same area. The monks at Key welcome visitors, and a bowl of butter tea in the courtyard is part of the experience.

The ride here is among the great ones. Whether you come from Shimla by way of Kinnaur or from Manali over the Kunzum La, the roads are rough, narrow and often unsurfaced, with water crossings, loose rock and drops that deserve respect. Altitude is a serious matter, and anyone who climbs too fast can feel headaches, nausea and breathlessness, so spend a day or two acclimatising. Weather can change in minutes, and the passes close with snow from late autumn into the early summer.

Kaza has the one fuel station that can be relied on for a very long way, and it sometimes runs short. Fill every tank and carry spare fuel. Cash machines are few and not always working, and mobile signal is patchy. Guest houses and homestays are simple and welcoming, and the food is mostly thukpa and momos.

The best time is late June to September, though the monsoon can cause landslides on the approach. In the clear light the mountains look close enough to touch.
t.leh@34.2,77.6:
Leh sits in the high desert of Ladakh at about 3,500 metres, in the broad valley of the Indus, with the Karakoram on one side and the Zanskar range on the other, and it is the end of the Manali-Leh highway, one of the great road journeys in the world. The last stage of that road is the best: you cross the Tanglang La, among the highest passes in the world, then drop to the Indus plain, through villages with whitewashed chortens and prayer flags, and the town appears below a hill crowned by the old Leh Palace, a nine-storey building of mud and wood modelled on the Potala in Lhasa. Behind it, the Namgyal Tsemo monastery and a ruined fort hang on the ridge.

Leh was a major stop on the caravan routes between India, Tibet and Central Asia, where traders brought pashmina, salt, silk and spices over the passes. The Buddhist heritage is strong and visible: the Shanti Stupa, built by Japanese monks, gives a grand view over the town, and monasteries such as Thiksey and Hemis stand within a day's ride, painted with bright murals. The old town below the palace has narrow lanes, and the main bazaar is full of Kashmiri and Tibetan craftwork.

The key to Leh is altitude, and it deserves respect. Spend at least two days there doing nothing before you ride higher, drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol on the first night and take headaches seriously, since acute mountain sickness can become dangerous. The sun is fierce, the air is thin and dry, and the nights are cold even in summer. For riders the roads to Khardung La, to Pangong Lake and to the Nubra Valley all start from here, and some of them need an Inner Line Permit, which can be arranged through a local agency or online. The riding season runs roughly from June to September, when the high roads are open, though landslides and snow can close them at any time.

The town has about thirty-seven thousand people, so fuel, mechanics, tyres and food are all available, but remember that the stations beyond Leh, in the Nubra and Pangong directions, are far apart, so carry a jerrycan for long days. Try thukpa, the noodle soup, momos and butter tea, and the apricots that grow in the valleys. Bakeries sell German-style cakes, a legacy of trekkers, and cafes on the main street have good coffee and views of the palace.
t.kargil@34.6,76.1:
Kargil sits at about 2,700 metres in the Suru valley in Ladakh, a town of tin roofs, apricot trees and mountains the colour of ash. Most travellers know it as a night stop on the road between Srinagar and Leh, which is about right, but it has a character of its own. Most of its people are Shia Muslims of Balti descent, and the call to prayer carries across the river valley beneath peaks that stay snowy for much of the year.

The town is also associated with the 1999 conflict between India and Pakistan, fought on the ridges above the highway, and there is a war memorial at Dras, about sixty kilometres to the west, that tells the story. Dras itself is known as one of the coldest inhabited places on earth, with winter temperatures that can plunge far below freezing. Before the war and the border closures, Kargil was a halt on the old caravan routes to Central Asia, and traders passed through with salt, tea and wool.

The highway here is one of the world's great rides. West of the town, it crosses the Zoji La from Kashmir, a narrow and often busy mountain pass, then follows the Dras and Suru rivers. East of Kargil, the road climbs through Mulbekh, with its carved Buddha statue, and over two passes, Namika La and Fotu La, the latter at over 4,000 metres, before reaching the monastery of Lamayuru, which sits above a barren landscape often called moonland. The road surface varies from good tarmac to rough, broken sections, with landslides common in monsoon and after snowmelt. The route is generally open from about May to October, and the Zoji La closes in winter. Altitude is a serious matter, so acclimatise and drink plenty of water.

Kargil has fuel, but supplies can be limited, and it is the last dependable fill-up for a long distance, so top up and carry a spare can. Simple guesthouses and restaurants serve rice, lentils, momos and strong sweet tea. Carry permits and documents, because checkpoints are routine, and start early, as afternoon winds and meltwater can complicate the road.
t.pang@33.1,77.8:
Pang is not a village so much as a seasonal camp, a straggle of tents and tea stalls on a bare high plateau in the Himalaya, and it earns its place on the Manali-Leh road by being where everyone wants to stop. The altitude is somewhere above 4,500 metres, which means the air carries about half the oxygen of sea level, and the first thing a rider notices is a thumping head and shortness of breath on any slope. Hot sweet tea and a plate of noodles taste better here than they have any right to.

The road to Pang from the south is a drama. After Sarchu the highway climbs the Gata Loops, a stack of twenty-one hairpin bends, and then crosses Nakee La and Lachulung La, the latter above 5,000 metres, before dropping to the plateau. Beyond Pang the road runs across the More Plains, a flat desert of pale gravel ringed by brown mountains, and then climbs again to Tanglang La, one of the highest motorable passes in the world at over 5,300 metres. The highway is maintained by the Border Roads Organisation, whose painted signs with cheerful slogans are part of the experience, though sections of surface are broken by meltwater, landslides and heavy trucks.

Altitude sickness is the real danger. Symptoms include headache, nausea, confusion and breathlessness, and they can become serious quickly. Climb slowly, drink water, eat lightly, and descend if you feel bad. Many travellers spend a night or two in Keylong or Leh to acclimatise before they ride this stretch. Temperatures swing from warm sun to freezing wind, and water crossings, where streams run over the road in the afternoon, can be deep and cold. Starting early is the best tactic, because meltwater rises as the day warms.

The road is open only in summer, usually from about June to September or early October, depending on snow. The tents are basic, with thick blankets, shared and cold, and meals are simple, usually dal, rice and noodles. Prepare for stars at night that look close enough to touch, and for cold that gets under every layer.
t.keylong@32.6,77.0:
Keylong is the main town of Lahaul, a high valley beyond the Rohtang Pass, and it sits at roughly three thousand metres above the Chandra and Bhaga rivers. For anyone riding north from Manali, this is the first real settlement after the climb, and the place where the road finally leaves the green side of the Himalaya and enters a drier, starker landscape. The mountains here are bare and brown, topped with snow, and the air is thin and clear.

Keylong has a distinctly Tibetan Buddhist character. Gompas, prayer flags and mani walls mark the area, and Kardang Monastery sits across the valley, an old centre of Buddhist learning. The town itself is small and practical, with a bazaar, some basic hotels and guesthouses, and a few places serving thukpa, momos and tea. It is not glamorous, but after the rough road from Manali it feels like a proper arrival, and many riders spend the night here to acclimatise.

The riding on the approach is about the surface as much as the corners. The road over Rohtang is often busy with trucks and tourist vehicles, and it is broken in many places by landslides, meltwater and rough patches. The pass itself is only open in the warmer months, usually from late spring into autumn, and heavy traffic in peak season can slow the climb significantly. The Atal Tunnel, which opened in 2020, now offers a faster way under the mountain, and reaching Lahaul has become much easier than it once was.

Fuel is available in Keylong, where there is a petrol pump that serves the whole valley, and it is the last reliable fill for a long stretch heading north, so top up fully. The next supply point is a long way up the road, and you should not assume anything will be available without checking. Carry water, extra layers and a basic repair kit, because the temperature can drop sharply and help is not always close.

Altitude matters here. Drink water, eat sensibly and take it slowly if you have come up quickly from Manali, because headaches and fatigue are common. Keylong is a good place to rest properly before the road gets higher and harder.
t.sarchu@33.0,77.6:
Sarchu is less a town than a seasonal camp, a flat, windswept plain at about four thousand metres on the border between Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh. There are no permanent villages here, only a scattering of tented camps and a few simple dhabas that open in the summer months for travellers on the Manali to Leh road. In the middle of the Himalaya it feels oddly open, ringed by pale mountains and crossed by a stream that comes down from the snow.

The place has long been a halfway point. Before the road was improved, drivers and travellers on this route usually broke the journey at Sarchu because the distances on either side were so long, and many still do. It sits between the Baralacha La and Lachulung La passes, so the ride in is a long climb through dry and treeless country, and the ride out involves the famous Gata Loops, a run of hairpins that climb steeply toward the next high pass.

Conditions are demanding. Altitude sickness is a real risk at this height, and sleeping at Sarchu is known to give people headaches and restless nights, so many riders prefer to push on to lower ground or stop earlier at Keylong. The weather can change within an hour, with wind, hail or snow arriving even in summer. Rivers cross the road in places, and meltwater makes the afternoon crossings deeper and more difficult than they are in the morning.

The nearest reliable supply to the south is at Keylong, and the next to the north is at Upshi or Leh, a very long way ahead, so riders carry extra fuel in cans or plan carefully around their range. Food and tea are available at the camps in season, basic but welcome. Do not count on cash machines or phone signal.

The road only opens in summer, normally from around June to September, and weather or landslides can close it without warning. Check before you set out. Sarchu is a place you pass through with respect rather than stay for comfort, but its emptiness has a strange beauty of its own.
t.sarchu@32.9,77.6:
Sarchu is not a town, and calling it a stop barely does it justice. It is a high, bare plateau at about 4,300 metres, on the boundary between Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh, where the Leh-Manali Highway crosses a wide, windy basin beside the Tsarap river. In the summer season, a collection of tents and camps appear on the plain, serving riders, truck drivers and travellers who need a place to sleep halfway between Manali and Leh, and in winter everything is gone and the snow takes over.

The history is longer than the camps. The route here follows an old trading path between Kullu, Lahaul and Ladakh, along which caravans carried wool, salt, pashmina and grain for centuries. Sarchu was a natural halting place, since the climb from either direction is long and the distances to the next shelter are great. The camps today have simple beds, warm blankets and hot food, usually dal, rice and tea, and they are well used, so expect company.

The riding is some of the most demanding in the world. From Manali the road climbs over the Rohtang and Baralacha La passes, with long stretches of broken tarmac, loose gravel, stream crossings and sharp drops, and after Sarchu come the Gata Loops, a sequence of twenty-one hairpin bends, and the long climb to Nakee La and Lachulung La. Mornings are best, as meltwater on the road freezes overnight and streams swell in the afternoon. The altitude is a danger in its own right: headaches, breathlessness and sleeplessness are common at Sarchu, so go slowly, drink water, and do not rush upward.

Fuel is the practical worry. There is no reliable pump at Sarchu itself, and the last known petrol station before the long gap is at Tandi, a day's ride south, so carry a reserve, and fill up at Karu, near Leh, when you arrive on the other side. Check the news and the road status before you leave, since landslides and snow can close the highway at short notice, and the season usually runs from June to September.

The night here is cold, often below freezing, and the stars are astonishing. Hearing the wind outside the tent and seeing the Milky Way over bare brown hills is the reason people come.
t.lachulung la@33.1,77.7:
Lachulung La is the second great pass on the road between Manali and Leh, a bare, windswept saddle at 5,059 metres, with prayer flags snapping in the wind and the road clawing its way over a ridge of crumbling rock. It lies north of Sarchu and the Gata Loops, in the high desert plateau of southern Ladakh, where the air is thin and the land is a bare, tawny colour streaked with red and green minerals. There are no trees and almost no plants, only rock, snow and sky.

The pass sits between the Nakee La and Tanglang La, forming the central part of a sequence of high crossings that makes the highway one of the highest in the world. Between them lie the More Plains, a wide flat basin at over 4,000 metres, where the road runs straight for miles across what feels like the surface of another planet. The area is sparsely populated, with a few nomadic herders and army posts, and the camps at Pang, to the south, serve those crossing the passes.

For riders the road is raw and unpredictable. The surface alternates between rough tarmac, broken sections, gravel and water crossings, and the gradients are steady rather than steep, but the thin air makes every bike, and every person, slower. Carburettor and injection engines lose power at altitude, and you may notice the bike feeling flat and sluggish, so be patient and avoid hard braking on loose surfaces. The weather can change in an hour, with sudden snow, hail or high wind, even in midsummer. Start early, to cross the passes before the afternoon meltwater, and carry warm layers.

The nearest supplies are at Pang and Sarchu to the south, and Upshi and Karu on the Leh side, and the long gap between pumps means a reserve of fuel is wise. Altitude sickness is the other danger: if you feel dizzy, nauseous or confused, lose height rather than gaining it.

Stop for a few minutes at the top, take a photograph with the prayer flags, but do not linger too long. The view across the folded ridges and distant snow peaks is wide and silent, and the satisfaction of crossing is real. After a brief rest, the road drops toward the Indus valley and Leh, and the air thickens with every kilometre.
t.dras@34.4,75.8:
Dras is a place of extremes, and the first thing to know is that it is cold. Sitting at about 3,200 metres in the high valley below Zoji La, it is often called the second coldest inhabited place in the world, and winter temperatures can plunge to somewhere around minus forty degrees. The snow falls heavily and stays for months, and the road from Kashmir is usually closed by the pass through the winter and early spring. In summer, though, the valley turns green, with barley fields and willows beside the river and the bare brown ranges rising on either side.

The ride into Dras from the west is a mighty one. You climb from the green meadows of Sonamarg to the narrow, crumbling track over Zoji La, where the road clings to the hillside above a huge drop and trucks and army convoys crawl in both directions. Much of the surface is broken, with mud, gravel and streams crossing the road, and the weather can change in an hour. After the pass, you descend into a barren, windy landscape that feels like a different planet, and Dras appears as a scattering of low houses in a wide valley.

Dras is also a sombre place. In 1999 the area was the scene of heavy fighting during the Kargil conflict, when Indian forces fought to retake peaks overlooking the highway, including Tololing and Tiger Hill, which are visible from the valley. A memorial to the soldiers who died stands beside the road, and its museum and lines of names are well worth a stop. The army is a constant presence, and you will pass many convoys and checkpoints.

Practical advice is essential. Fuel is scarce, so fill the tank at Sonamarg or take spare fuel and plan to reach Kargil, about sixty kilometres to the east. Simple tea stalls and dhabas serve hot food and sweet tea, which is welcome in the wind. The altitude can cause headaches, so drink water and go slowly. The best time to come is from June to September, when the road is open and the weather mild, but even then mornings are cold, and a warm jacket and gloves are essential, with rain gear in the panniers.
t.atal tunnel north portal@32.4,77.2:
The Atal Tunnel changed the Himalayan road map. For generations, the road north from Manali climbed over the Rohtang Pass, which was open for only part of the year, snowed in from late autumn to early summer. In 2020 a tunnel of about nine kilometres was opened under the pass, one of the longest highway tunnels in the world at such a height, and named after the former prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee. The north portal, where you emerge into Lahaul, is one of the great moments on the road to Ladakh.

The contrast is striking. On the Manali side the valley is wet, green and wooded, with pine and deodar forests and apple orchards. When you come out of the tunnel's north end, you find a drier, harsher world: bare slopes of scree and rock, a few poplar-lined villages, and the Chandra River running through a broad glacial valley. The light is sharper, the sky is bluer, and the air is thinner. The Lahaul valley lies in the rain shadow of the Pir Panjal range, so it gets much less monsoon rain than the south side, which is why it has become a popular route in July and August when the rest of the Himalayas are soaked.

The road beyond the portal is generally good, with long curves and a wide surface, and it follows the river towards Keylong, the district headquarters, some thirty kilometres further on. Traffic can be heavy with trucks and tourist vehicles, and the tunnel itself has speed limits and no overtaking, so be patient. The tunnel is not immune to snow and avalanche, and it can close in bad conditions, so check the latest news.

Simple restaurants at Sissu and Keylong offer dal, rice and tea. The height here is around three thousand metres, and acclimatisation is wise. The best months are June to September, when the roads are open and the air is warm, and the waterfall at Sissu is a reason to stop.
t.baralacha la@32.7,77.4:
Baralacha La is a pass that feels like the roof of the world, and at 4,890 metres, it nearly is. The name means the pass with crossroads on the summit, because it sits where roads from Lahaul, Zanskar and Ladakh once met. The rivers tell the story: the Chandra rises near here on the south side, and the Yunam flows north, and a few kilometres below the pass lies the clear, round lake of Suraj Tal, one of the highest lakes in India, from which the Bhaga River begins.

The riding on the Leh–Manali road is dramatic but demanding. The tarmac is mostly good on the south side, with long, graded curves, but it breaks up into gravel and mud where snowmelt streams cross it, and in places the road is a rough track. At altitude, the engine is short of air and the rider is short of breath, so go slowly, drink plenty of water and be ready to stop if your head aches. The landscape is spectacular, with red and orange mountains, snowfields and glaciers, and a huge sky. Weather can change from sun to snow in minutes, even in summer.

The pass is open only in summer, usually from around June until September or October, depending on the snow, and the road is often closed by landslides or heavy snow. Basic tented camps and tea stalls operate in summer, but they come and go, and you should carry food, water and warm clothes.

The silence on the summit is memorable. A cold wind blows over the stones, prayer flags snap, and there is a sense of being a very long way from anywhere. The Himalayan marmots whistle among the rocks, and you may see herds of sheep and goats driven up from the villages for the summer grass. Take care to rest at the lower camp, because sleeping high is when altitude sickness is most likely to hit. For a rider, it is a place that demands respect and rewards it with views that stay with you.
t.tanglang la@33.2,77.8:
Tanglang La is the second highest of the great passes on the road between Manali and Leh, at about 5,300 metres, and it is a place where the air is so thin that walking up a few steps feels like climbing a stair. The pass lies on the watershed between the Indus valley and the high plateau to the south, and the landscape around it is stark and vast: bare ridges of brown and grey, snowfields in the shadows, and a sky that looks very dark and very close.

The ride up from the south crosses the Morey Plains, a high, flat desert at nearly four and a half thousand metres, which is an astonishing place in itself. The road runs across it in long, straight lines, with the surface sometimes smooth and sometimes broken, and the mountains standing at the edges like the walls of a vast amphitheatre. Then the road begins to climb in a series of bends to the summit, where you will find a signboard, a heap of prayer flags and perhaps a few other riders taking photographs.

On the north side, the road drops steeply towards the Indus, passing the village of Rumtse, where the first green returns. Leh is roughly a hundred kilometres from the pass, and the descent into the valley is a long, welcome relief to the lungs. The road here is generally good, with big curves and open views, but be ready for sudden gusts of wind and the odd landslide.

Practical matters are serious at this height. Tents at Pang, on the southern approach, offer simple meals and a bed, but they are basic and the nights are bitterly cold. Spend a few days in Leh before attempting the pass, drink lots of water and stay a short time at the summit, because altitude sickness is real and can strike without warning. The season runs from June to September, and the pass can close at any time with snow.
t.great living chola temples@10.8,79.1:
The Cauvery delta is the rice bowl of Tamil Nadu, and for a thousand years it fed an empire. The Cholas, who ruled much of southern India from the ninth to the thirteenth century, built their power on the fields, the ports and the fleet that carried their armies as far as Sumatra, and they poured their wealth into temples. Three of these, the Brihadisvara at Thanjavur, the one at Gangaikonda Cholapuram and the Airavatesvara at Darasuram, are together a UNESCO World Heritage site, the Great Living Chola Temples, and the adjective is accurate: priests still perform rites in them daily.

Thanjavur, also called Tanjore, is a city of about 220,000, with a Maratha palace, a famous library of old manuscripts, and a workshop tradition of bronze casting and painted panels with gold leaf. Musicians still make veenas, the stringed instrument of south Indian classical music, in the streets near the temple. Fuel and food are easy to find, and the city is a convenient base for exploring the delta, with the town of Kumbakonam, where the Airavatesvara temple stands nearby, a short ride away.

The riding is flat and straightforward. Roads run between flooded paddy fields, banana groves and coconut palms, with villages every few kilometres and wayside shrines in between. Traffic is heavy, with buses, lorries and tractors, and the roads can be rough. Long straight stretches are broken by sudden speed bumps, and cattle wander on the verge. The heat is considerable, especially from April to June, and the best time to ride is from November to February, when the days are mild.

Food is a pleasure, with banana-leaf meals of rice, lentils, curries and pickles served at simple restaurants, and strong filter coffee in small steel cups. In the early morning, the temple's great tower catches the first light, and the town is quiet, with the smell of incense and jasmine in the air.
The great tower of the Brihadisvara temple dominates Thanjavur like a mountain made by hand. Built by the Chola king Rajaraja I and completed around 1010, it rises about 66 metres in thirteen tiers, and its summit is crowned by a single block of granite that tradition says weighs eighty tonnes. Stories say that the builders raised an earthen ramp for several kilometres to haul it into place, though how they did so remains a puzzle that guides enjoy debating. A local legend adds that at noon the tower casts no shadow on the ground, which is a nice tale rather than a fact.

The temple is made entirely of granite, a stone that does not occur near Thanjavur, and the blocks must have been brought from quarries some distance away. Inside the courtyard, a huge Nandi, the sacred bull of Shiva, sits facing the sanctuary, carved from a single rock, and the walls are covered with inscriptions and carvings that record the gifts, the dancers and the musicians who served the temple. It is a place of worship in daily use, with priests, lamps, flowers and the sound of bells, and visitors are asked to dress modestly and remove their shoes.

Thanjavur, about 220,000 people, has fuel, food and places to stay, and the temple is easily reached from the centre. Parking for motorcycles is available near the entrance, and the courtyard is open from morning to evening, with a break at midday. The paving stones get very hot in the afternoon, so bring socks or go early.

The temple is part of the Great Living Chola Temples, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Evening is the best time, when the heat has lifted, the stone glows red-gold, and families gather on the lawns. It is easy to sit for an hour, watching the light change, and to feel the scale of what a medieval dynasty could achieve.
t.reckong peo@31.5,78.3:
Reckong Peo is the district headquarters of Kinnaur, in the Indian state of Himachal Pradesh, and it sits on the old Hindustan-Tibet Road, a route that clings to the walls of the Sutlej gorge. The town is at roughly 2,700 metres, among apple orchards and pine, and the peak that dominates the view is Kinner Kailash, a rocky, glittering mountain of about 6,000 metres that is sacred to Hindus and Buddhists. On a clear morning the first light on its flanks is something to see.

The ride up to here is dramatic in itself. The road follows the Sutlej river from Shimla through some of the steepest country in the western Himalaya, with cliffs overhead, hairpins beside the drop and long stretches that are carved into bare rock. Landslides are common, especially during the monsoon, so check conditions and be prepared for delays. Mornings are generally clearer, and the surface can be broken, with loose stones and water running across the road.

Above the town is Kalpa, a quieter village with wooden houses and Buddhist and Hindu temples, which is where many riders choose to stay for the view. Kinnaur is known for apples, apricots and the chilgoza pine, whose nuts are a local delicacy. The valley has a unique culture that blends Hindu and Buddhist traditions, with its own dialects and its own distinctive woollen caps.

Practical matters count here. Reckong Peo has fuel, shops, banks and places to eat, and it is the last large settlement before the remote Spiti valley. Fuel further on is limited, with the main station at Kaza, so fill the tank and carry spare if your bike has a small range. Carry cash, check permit requirements for the border areas before you set off, and allow plenty of time, because distances here are measured in hours, not kilometres.

The Spiti Valley circuit starts here, and this is the moment to check tyres, brakes and luggage. After this the road climbs toward Nako and the cold desert, and the lush green apple orchards give way to bare, windswept mountains.
t.fotu la@34.3,76.9:
Fotu La is the highest point on the road between Srinagar and Leh, at 4,108 metres, and it is higher than the better-known Namika La further west. It is a broad, windswept saddle with prayer flags snapping in the wind, a few signs from the Border Roads Organisation and a feeling of enormous space. The altitude is real, so do not be surprised if a short walk makes you breathless; take your time and drink plenty of water.

The pass lies in Ladakh, in the stretch of high desert between Mulbekh and Lamayuru, with bare, wrinkled mountains in shades of brown, ochre and grey. The ride is in good condition for much of the way, with smooth, wide tarmac and long, easy hairpins on the ascent and descent, although there are stretches of broken surface where meltwater or rockfall has taken its toll. Frequent army convoys, trucks and tourist vehicles share the road, so be patient, and watch for sudden gusts of wind and a drop in temperature even on sunny days.

Below the pass on the eastern side lies Lamayuru, one of the oldest and most spectacular monasteries in Ladakh, perched on a cliff above a landscape of eroded, pale clay formations that people call moonland. It is a worthwhile stop if you have time. Further west, Mulbekh has a large carved statue of Maitreya, the future Buddha, standing beside the road, and the Buddhist culture of Ladakh grows stronger as you approach Leh.

Fill up at Kargil, or in Leh, and consider carrying a spare can, because stations on this route can run dry and distances between them are considerable. Food stops are simple, with dhaba tea stalls and momos in small villages, but they are friendly and welcome.

The road is generally open between late spring and autumn, closing when heavy snow arrives, and the Zoji La, further west, is often the real bottleneck. Check conditions before you go, and aim to cross the pass in the morning, before the afternoon wind picks up.
t.morro do pai inacio@-12.5,-41.5:
Morro do Pai Inácio is a flat-topped hill that rises out of the scrub of the Chapada Diamantina in the interior of Bahia, standing a little above a thousand metres. It is the sort of place where the earth seems to have been cut and left. The sandstone plateaus of this region, called chapadas, are ancient, eroded into cliffs, canyons and tabletop hills, and the Morro is one of the most photographed. From the top, a short, steep walk of perhaps fifteen minutes from the road, you look out over the valley of the Rio Utinga and the plateaus beyond, in a view that stretches to the horizon.

The legend is dramatic. Pai Inácio was an enslaved man who, so the story goes, escaped his master and was cornered on the hill. Rather than be taken, he jumped off with an umbrella, and a gust of wind carried him down safely, while the pursuers thought he had died. Whether it is true or not, the hill carries his name, and the legend is told to every visitor. The region was a centre of diamond mining in the nineteenth century, hence its name, and the old mining towns, like Lençóis, have colonial buildings that survive from those days.

The road here, the BR-242, runs through a landscape of dry scrub and rocky outcrops, with long straight sections and gentle bends. The surface is generally good, though potholes and road repairs appear, and trucks and buses share the route. It is hot in the day, and the red earth, the sandstone and the cactus give the place a strong, dry character. Dusk is the best time to be on top of the Morro, when the sun lights the plateau in gold and pink, though you should plan the descent in the fading light and carry a torch.

Fuel is the main practical concern. The nearest stations are at Iraquara, about twenty-eight kilometres away, and Seabra, a little further, so fill up before reaching the hill. Iraquara is the gateway to some of the region's caves, including the Gruta da Lapa Doce and the Poço Azul, where underground pools of clear blue water can be seen. Visitors often start tours at Lençóis, a short ride down the road. The dry season, from about May to September, is the most comfortable. Take water and sun protection, because there is little shade on the hilltop.
t.ibicoara@-13.4,-41.3:
Ibicoara is a small town at the southern end of the Chapada Diamantina, in the highlands of Bahia, far from the more touristy centre around Lençóis. The town sits at a cool altitude, which makes it good for growing coffee, and the hillsides around are covered with plantations, as well as potatoes and other vegetables. It is known for its waterfalls, in particular the Cachoeira do Buracão, an eighty-five-metre cascade that drops into a great rock amphitheatre, reached by a walk and a swim across a pool, and often described as one of the most beautiful in the region.

The surrounding landscape is the old sandstone plateau, cut by rivers and falling away in cliffs, with a mixture of dry scrub, rocky grassland and patches of forest. Much of it lies within the Chapada Diamantina National Park, which protects a large area of mountains, caves and waterfalls. The air is clean and cool in the mornings, and at night the stars are brilliant. Birdlife is rich, and the call of the toucan can be heard in the trees.

The ride to Ibicoara from the north takes you across a high plain where the road runs straight and the landscape rolls away to far horizons. Surfaces are variable: some stretches are well paved and others have potholes, and the last part to the falls may be on unpaved tracks that are slippery when wet. Check conditions locally before setting off. Traffic is light, but trucks and animals on the road, particularly at dusk, are a hazard, and wide gravel verges can be loose.

Barra da Estiva is the nearest larger town, twenty-four kilometres away, with fuel stations, shops and restaurants, so fill up there. Ibicoara itself has small hotels, family-run restaurants and a few shops. The local food is simple and good: rice and beans with grilled meat and farofa, fresh coffee and cake in the afternoon. The region was important in the diamond rush of the nineteenth century, and the old trails of the garimpeiros, the prospectors, can still be walked. The best season for waterfalls is just after the rains, in the early months of the year, but the dry months from May to September are easier for riding.
t.south pullu@34.2,77.6:
South Pullu is a checkpoint rather than a destination, a bend on the long climb out of Leh where the army has set up a post and where the road leaves the last of the valley behind and begins to go seriously uphill. It sits on the Leh side of Khardung La, within a short run of the city, and for many riders it is the first moment of the day when the altitude begins to announce itself. Leh is at about 3,500 metres, and the road from here keeps climbing for another stretch of about twenty-odd kilometres before it reaches the pass.

The riding in this section is the build-up. The road leaves the Indus valley, switches back across barren mountainside, and the surface is a mix of fine tarmac, broken patches, and spots where meltwater has crossed the road and left grit and mud. The landscape is desert, brown and grey rock with no trees, and the light at this height is hard and clear. Weather matters a great deal. The pass itself can be in cloud or snow while Leh is sunny, and in the afternoon the road often turns slushy as snowmelt runs across it.

This is also where you meet the paperwork. Visitors going over the pass towards Nubra need the correct permit, which is arranged in Leh, and the army posts check them. Keep copies handy, and have your riding documents ready. The soldiers here are generally courteous, and a short stop for a form and a chat is a routine part of the trip.

Fuel is a real consideration. Fill the tank in Leh before you set off, as there is nothing on the climb and the thin air takes a toll on engines, particularly carburetted bikes that lose power as the oxygen drops. Carry a spare litre or two if you can, and know that Diskit, on the far side, has fuel but can run short in peak season. Carry water, and eat something before you go, because altitude and an empty stomach make for a miserable mix.

Early starts are the best strategy. Leave Leh soon after dawn, clear the post with the road mostly frozen and firm, and you will cross the pass with the cleaner morning air and less melt on the tarmac.
t.khardung la@34.3,77.6:
Khardung La stands at 5,359 metres by the figure in the data, though the signs on the pass itself claim a higher number, and the argument over its exact height has become part of its charm. It was opened to the public in the late 1980s, and for years it was marketed as the highest motorable road in the world. Whatever the real statistics, you are riding through air with roughly half the oxygen of sea level, and every motorcyclist who gets here has a story about it.

The road from Leh is a steady climb of about forty kilometres, mostly on tarmac that ranges from good to terrible. The upper section is where things get serious. Snow can lie at the roadside well into summer, meltwater crosses the road in streams, and the surface turns to mud and loose stone in places. The Border Roads Organisation keeps the route open, and its signs, with their dry jokes about speed and safety, are a feature of the whole climb. Be careful on the descent too, because brakes and nerves take a pounding.

At the top there is a cluster of prayer flags, a small cafe and a shrine run by the army, and a sign you will want a photo with. Stay no more than about twenty minutes. The altitude can hit hard and fast, with headaches, nausea and dizziness, and the right response is to descend, not to push on. If you have not acclimatised in Leh for at least two days, you are asking for trouble. Drink water, breathe slowly, and do not be the rider who tries to prove something.

The surrounding mountains are of the Ladakh range, and on a clear day the view across to the Karakoram is huge and quiet. The weather, however, is the real boss. It can be bright and still, then snowing within the hour, and the pass is sometimes closed for hours or days after storms. Winter closures are common, though the army works to clear the road.

Leh, around thirteen kilometres by straight line and much further by road, is where you fill up, and the next dependable supply is on the far side in the Nubra valley. Carry water, warm gloves and a windproof layer, and start early.
t.north pullu@34.3,77.7:
North Pullu is the second checkpoint on the Khardung La road, on the Nubra side of the pass, and it marks the point where the descent begins to feel like a reward. After the thin air and the broken surfaces of the summit, the road drops into a different country, and the valley below takes shape as a long, pale stripe of green in the brown mountains. The checkpoint itself is small, a few buildings and an army post, but riders tend to remember it because they are usually glad to be heading downhill.

The descent is long, steep and demanding. The road is a ribbon of tight bends cut into slopes of loose rock, and the surface varies from decent tarmac to patches of gravel and washouts where streams cross. The brakes get a thorough workout, so engine braking in a low gear is the sensible approach, and nobody who has been through here forgets the long sections of switchbacks. Rockfall and landslides happen, especially in warmer months when meltwater loosens the slopes. Expect trucks, army convoys and the occasional herd of animals on the tarmac.

Papers are checked here, as at South Pullu, so keep your permit and documents handy. The soldiers will often ask where you are headed and may offer tea if the weather is cold, an old Himalayan courtesy that has survived the modern checkpoints. As you drop, the temperature climbs noticeably, and layers you needed at the top become a burden a few thousand feet lower. Stop somewhere safe to adjust.

Nubra has its own pumps, with Diskit the main supply point, but availability can be patchy at busy times, so start with a full tank from Leh and treat anything beyond it as a bonus. Tea stalls and small cafes appear as you get lower, and the first villages bring the first real food on the far side.

What you notice most as you descend is the change in scale. The big, bare Ladakh peaks give way to willow, poplar and apricot trees, then the sand and braided streams of the Shyok and Nubra rivers. After the stark top of the world, this feels almost gentle, and the sense of relief is as much a part of the experience as the pass itself.
t.diskit@34.6,77.6:
Diskit is the main town of the Nubra valley, a spread of low buildings along the Shyok river with a monastery perched above on a rock. The valley sits north of Leh, beyond the great hurdle of Khardung La, and its low altitude, around three thousand metres, makes it feel almost lush after the pass. Willows, poplars, wild rose and sea buckthorn line the river, and in the right season the fields turn bright green against the dry, pale mountains that surround them.

The Diskit Gompa is the oldest and largest Buddhist monastery in the valley, belonging to the Gelugpa school, and its whitewashed buildings climb a spur above the town in a stack of rooms, courtyards and prayer halls. It dates back several centuries and is worth the short climb up. On a nearby hill, a large statue of Maitreya, the future Buddha, looks out over the valley, completed in the early 2010s, and the view from its feet sweeps across the river plain toward the Karakoram foothills.

A few kilometres on, the village of Hunder has sand dunes and a small herd of two-humped Bactrian camels, descendants of animals once used on the caravan routes between Ladakh and Central Asia. Nubra was part of those trade routes, which crossed the Karakoram Pass into what is now Xinjiang. Many riders stop in Diskit or Hunder for the night, and there are guesthouses and camps of all kinds, plus small restaurants serving momos, thukpa and strong, sweet tea.

The riding in the valley is easy compared with the descent from Khardung La. The roads are mostly paved, the gradients gentle, and the scenery is open and big, though the wind can pick up in the afternoons and throw sand across the tarmac. Watch for dogs, cattle and the occasional army truck.

Diskit has a petrol pump, which is the main source of fuel for the valley, but supply can run short in peak season, and some visitors have found it empty. It is wise to fill in Leh before going over the pass and treat Diskit as a backup. Evenings are cool, even in summer, and nights can be cold, so pack a warm layer.

If you are lucky with the weather, the morning light on the monastery and the river is one of the best sights in Ladakh.
t.turtuk@34.8,76.8:
Turtuk is the last village in India before the Line of Control, and it feels like the end of a long road in every sense. It sits in the Shyok valley in the far north of Ladakh, under the Karakoram, at a lower altitude than Leh, which makes it warm enough for apricots, walnuts and barley. Until 1971 it was part of Pakistan, and it was only opened to visitors in 2010. The people are Balti, Muslim, and their language and food are closer to Baltistan than to the Buddhist world of central Ladakh, which gives the place a character all its own. There is little population nearby: the nearest settlement of any size is the hamlet of Thang, about nine kilometres away.

The ride arrives after the long haul over Khardung La and down the Nubra valley, then along the Shyok river. The road is narrow, mostly paved but with sections of broken surface, rockfalls and water crossings, depending on the season. The mountains are enormous and bare, in shades of ochre, grey and red, and the river is milky with glacial silt. The road passes army posts, so keep your permits and ID handy, and do not photograph military installations.

Turtuk is one of the great surprises of the route. After days of cold desert, you arrive among green terraces, stone houses with flat roofs and the sound of running water in channels. Apricots dry on the rooftops in late summer, and there is a small museum about the Balti way of life. Do not expect big infrastructure: fuel is a real concern, as there is nothing reliable in the village, so fill in Diskit or Hunder and carry spare if your bike has a small tank. Homestays serve simple meals of rice, vegetables and butter tea.

The season is short, roughly June to September, as the passes close under snow in winter and landslides can cut the road in summer. Mornings are cold, afternoons warm, and the altitude, though lower than Khardung La at over five thousand metres, still demands care. It is a place where the effort of getting there is part of the story, and the quiet at the end feels earned.
t.mysuru@12.3,76.6:
Mysuru, still called Mysore in many mouths, is the former capital of the Wodeyar kings and one of the easiest big cities in India to like. With about nine hundred thousand people it is large, but it moves at a gentler pace than Bengaluru, and the centre is built around the Mysore Palace, a huge Indo-Saracenic building that is lit by about a hundred thousand bulbs on Sundays and during the Dasara festival. The wide avenues, old markets and sandalwood stalls give the city its character. Sandalwood soap and silk are local products, and Mysore pak, a sweet made of gram flour, ghee and sugar, was invented in the palace kitchens.

As a start for a ride toward the Nilgiris, it works very well. Fuel is everywhere, hotels are plentiful, and the road southwest is wide and mostly smooth. Leave early, because Karnataka traffic builds quickly, with trucks, buses, auto-rickshaws and the occasional cow. The first stretch passes through flat farmland of sugarcane and banana, then enters forest as you approach Bandipur and Mudumalai, where the road becomes part of tiger and elephant country.

That wildlife corridor changes the riding. Bandipur National Park has night restrictions on traffic on the main road, so you must reach and cross it in daylight, and speed limits are strict, with checkpoints at the forest boundaries. Elephants cross the road without hurry and they are not to be tested. Slow down for monkeys and deer, and never feed them. The road is a fine ride in the early morning, when mist hangs over the trees and birds are loud.

Before leaving Mysuru, give yourself an hour for breakfast: masala dosa, idli with sambar, and filter coffee in a steel tumbler are typical, and the older cafes near the market are worth finding. The best months to ride are October to February, when the air is cool and dry; the monsoon from June to September brings heavy rain and slippery roads. From here, the road begins to climb toward Ooty and the blue hills.
t.bandipur@11.7,76.6:
The forest begins quite suddenly. One moment you are in the farmland around Gundlupet, with sunflower and marigold fields stretching to the horizon, and the next the road runs into dry deciduous woodland, and the signs warn you about elephants. Bandipur is a tiger reserve in southern Karnataka, joined along its border to the Mudumalai reserve in Tamil Nadu and the Wayanad forests in Kerala, and together they form one of the largest protected tracts of forest in India. The highway from Mysuru to Ooty cuts straight through it, which is why this ride feels more like a safari than a commute.

The road is a good one, wide and mostly well surfaced, with gentle bends through teak, bamboo and tall grass. You are riding through habitat, not along its edge. Chital deer are the common sight, grazing in small herds at the verge. Langurs sit on the tarmac like commuters waiting for a bus, peacocks stalk through the undergrowth, and with a bit of luck you will see gaur, the huge Indian bison, or a wild elephant standing in the shade. Tigers live here too, but they keep to themselves, and anyone who claims to have seen one from the highway has had a very lucky day.

There are rules and they matter. Traffic through the reserve is banned at night, roughly from nine in the evening until six in the morning, to protect wildlife, so plan your day to be through before dark. Do not stop to feed or photograph animals at close range, and do not leave rubbish. A wild elephant can be very dangerous, especially a bull in musth or a mother with a calf, so slow down if you see one near the road and keep a gap to turn away if it moves. Speed limits are low and enforced, and the checkpoint staff are used to explaining them to impatient visitors.

The air changes as you climb out of the forest, with the scent of dry leaves and dust giving way to cooler, damper air at the foot of the Nilgiri hills. March to May is hot and dry, when animals gather near the water and are easiest to see. The monsoon turns the woods emerald but can bring leeches and heavy showers.

Fuel is not available inside the forest. Gundlupet, a larger town with pumps and food stalls, is the last sensible place to fill up, with Masinigudi on the Tamil Nadu side a smaller alternative. Eat before you enter, because the forest stretch has little more than the odd tea stall.
t.gudalur@11.5,76.5:
Gudalur is the sort of place you pass through without noticing until you need it. It is a busy market town on the western edge of the Nilgiris, in Tamil Nadu, where roads from Mysuru, Ooty and the Kerala coast meet at a crowded junction of buses, jeeps and tea lorries. The surrounding hills are covered in plantations: tea on the slopes, coffee and pepper in the shade, with cardamom and rubber lower down. The air smells of damp earth and wood smoke, and the light has a green, filtered quality, especially in monsoon season when low cloud hangs over the ridges.

The town sits at a lower altitude than Ooty, and the road to the main hill station climbs by way of Naduvattam, a long, winding ascent through tea estates and eucalyptus. This is a proper hill road, with tight bends, steep gradients and views that open suddenly where the trees part. The surface is generally good but patched, and heavy rain can leave water, mud and fallen branches across the tarmac. Trucks and buses grind uphill at walking pace on some sections, and overtaking is a game of patience and horn. Early morning mist is common and visibility can be poor, so lights on and a steady pace make sense.

Gudalur has the practical things, which is why it matters. There are petrol pumps, small restaurants serving south Indian meals on banana leaf, strong coffee and sweet tea, and plenty of places to buy water and snacks. After the forest sections of the Mysuru road, with no services and a night ban, it is a relief to come out into a town where everything is for sale. Prices are low and portions generous, and a simple plate of rice, sambar and a few vegetable curries makes a good lunch.

Culturally the area is mixed, with Tamil, Malayali and indigenous communities living side by side, and the plantation history goes back to the British, who cleared the forest for tea in the nineteenth century. Elephants still wander through the estates at night, so avoid riding in the dark, and be careful on early morning descents where animals may be crossing.

The best months are probably October to March, when the rains have eased and the air is cool. In the monsoon the road becomes slick, and leeches turn up in the wet undergrowth, though the scenery is at its most dramatic.
t.ooty@11.4,76.7:
Ooty is the queen of the Nilgiris in the way that British hill stations liked to be queens, which is to say it is cool, slightly eccentric and wildly overcrowded at the weekend. Its official name is Udhagamandalam, and it sits at roughly 2,240 metres on a plateau in the Blue Mountains of Tamil Nadu. In the nineteenth century it was the summer capital of the Madras Presidency, and the colonial administrators built churches, clubs, cottages and a famous botanical garden in a landscape that reminded them of home. The hills were originally the territory of the Toda people, pastoralists with their own customs and beautiful barrel-vaulted huts, and some communities still live in the surrounding hills.

For motorcyclists the appeal is in the approach. Whichever way you come, the road climbs through tea, eucalyptus and pine, with the temperature dropping at every hairpin, and the final arrival in a town of nearly a hundred thousand people is a little anticlimactic. The centre is a tangle of narrow streets, one-way systems and honking traffic, particularly in May and during school holidays. Park the bike and walk if you want to see anything. The lake, the botanical gardens, the racecourse and the old church are all within reach, and the town's tea shops and bakeries sell fresh bread, cakes and homemade chocolate.

Do take the time to ride the Nilgiri Mountain Railway by eye, if not by seat. The narrow-gauge rack-and-pinion line runs from Mettupalayam through Coonoor to Ooty, and it is one of the UNESCO-listed mountain railways of India. You will cross its path several times if you come up the Coonoor road, and a steam engine puffing past in the mist is a glorious sight.

Fuel and food are no problem here, with pumps on the main roads and plenty of restaurants. Hotels are numerous but fill up quickly in the high season, so book ahead if you plan to stay overnight. Nights can be cold, even in summer, and in winter frost occurs on the higher ground, so pack a jacket.

The best months to ride are October to February for clear skies and cool air, and the mornings are the best time of day, before the traffic fills the lanes. In the monsoon the whole district disappears into cloud and rain, which has its own moody charm if you do not mind getting wet.
t.coonoor@11.4,76.8:
Coonoor is the quieter sister of Ooty, and most riders who know both prefer it. It sits at about 1,800 metres on the Nilgiri plateau in Tamil Nadu, on the slopes above a deep valley, and it lives on tea. Plantations cover the hills around the town in neat green ridges, with pickers moving between the rows, and factories along the roads sell fresh leaf and chocolate. The army town of Wellington lies right next door, a little under two kilometres away, and Kotagiri is ten kilometres on. Coonoor itself has fuel pumps and everything else you need.

The ride up from the plains is the real event. After the heat of the flatlands, the road climbs the ghats in a long series of hairpins through forest and plantation, and the temperature drops noticeably as you rise. Monkeys sit on the walls and buses take the corners wide, so go carefully on the blind ones. Mist and rain appear quickly, especially in the monsoon, and the surface can be greasy under the trees. A cold, fresh morning in winter is the finest time, when the views across the valleys are clear.

Coonoor has colonial roots. British officers and administrators built bungalows and churches here to escape the summer heat, and the Nilgiri Mountain Railway, a rack-and-pinion line that is a UNESCO World Heritage site, still climbs up from Mettupalayam, with old steam locomotives on part of the run. Sim's Park, a botanical garden laid out in the 1870s, is a pleasant place to rest, and Dolphin's Nose viewpoint looks down a huge drop.

For food, try the local tea at a roadside stall, and eat dosas, parottas or a plain thali in town. The air smells of eucalyptus and wet earth, which is the real smell of the Nilgiris. The hills have a long tradition of tea, and the Nilgiri variety is light, fragrant and good with milk or without. If you can, stay a night and walk among the bushes at dawn, when the whole plateau looks scrubbed clean.
t.manali@32.2,77.2:
Manali is where the plains give up and the Himalaya begins in earnest. The town sits in the Kullu valley in Himachal Pradesh, on the banks of the Beas, among deodar forests and apple orchards, with snow peaks rising behind. Old Manali, across the river, is the quieter half, a tangle of lanes, wooden houses and cafes, and in the cedar woods above the town stands the Hadimba temple, a pagoda-like wooden shrine built in the sixteenth century and dedicated to a figure from the Mahabharata. The valley has long been a stopping place for traders, travellers and, more recently, backpackers and motorcyclists.

For riders, Manali is the gateway to some of the most famous roads in the world. The Spiti Valley circuit sets out from here, climbing through the Atal Tunnel, a nine-kilometre bore under the Rohtang Pass that opened in 2020 and cut hours off the journey to Lahaul. Beyond lie high, bare mountain roads, river crossings, landslide sections and passes over four thousand metres, including Kunzum La at about 4,550 metres, the entrance to Spiti. The surface can be broken and muddy, and conditions change quickly, with snow possible even in summer. The season runs roughly from June to October, and many high roads close in winter.

Manali has a few thousand people, plus thousands of seasonal visitors, so fuel, workshops and food are plentiful. Nagar, a smaller town about eleven kilometres away, has an old castle with a view of the valley. Fill the tank and take spare fuel in a container before leaving, since stations on the Spiti route are few and far between, with Kaza the main supply point inside the valley. Altitude is a serious matter, so acclimatise, drink water and listen to your body.

The food in Manali is a pleasure, from momos and thukpa to trout from the Beas, and the sun in the morning is warm even when the air is cold. Rise early, because the road is quietest then, and the light on the snow peaks is magical. Carry warm clothing, and always tell someone where you are going.
t.eravikulam national park@10.2,77.2:
Anamudi is the highest mountain in India south of the Himalaya, and it rises from the Eravikulam plateau like a dark tooth. The national park, in the high Western Ghats near Munnar in Kerala, protects a landscape of rolling grassland, thick shola forest in the folds of the hills, and open skies, at heights above two thousand metres. It forms part of the Western Ghats World Heritage Site, inscribed by UNESCO in 2012, and it is the best place in the world to see the Nilgiri tahr, a stocky wild goat that lives on steep, grassy slopes.

The tahr were once close to extinction, shot for sport and driven from their ranges, and the park was set up largely to save them. They now number in the hundreds here and are remarkably tame, grazing within a few metres of the path. The plateau is also famous for the neelakurinji, a shrub that flowers purple-blue once every twelve years, covering the hills in a haze of colour. It last bloomed in 2018 and will do so again in about 2030, and the Munnar region fills with visitors when it does.

Munnar is a tea town, and the roads that climb to it from the plains run through endless terraced estates, green and tidy, with pickers working among the bushes and tea factories at the roadsides. The road is a series of hairpins up the ghats, with thick mist, sudden showers, and the cool, damp air that makes the tea so good. Surfaces can be broken after rain, and the monsoon, from June to August, brings landslides and heavy cloud.

Visitors can enter only the lower section of the park, by park-run bus from the entrance at Rajamalai, and the park is closed in February and March for the tahr calving season, so check before you plan a visit. Come early in the day, bring a rain jacket and wear layers, since the wind on the plateau is cold.

Marayur, seven kilometres away, is known for its sandalwood forests and dolmens, and offers fuel and a few places to eat. Munnar has more, but fill up on the way if you can.
t.kunzum pass@32.4,77.6:
At 4,551 metres, Kunzum Pass is the gate between two worlds. On one side lies Lahaul, with the Chandra river and the green fringes of the Himalayan monsoon. On the other side lies Spiti, a high, dry cold desert where the mountains are bare and brown, the sky is absurdly blue, and villages sit in oases on the valley floor. The pass is the only road link between the two valleys, and it is closed by snow for much of the year, usually opening around June and shutting again by October or earlier.

At the top, there is a small shrine to Kunzum Mata, a local deity, with a cairn of stones and strings of prayer flags snapping in the wind. Riders and drivers traditionally circle it clockwise before going on, and it feels right to do it. The view across the glaciers and peaks of the Lahaul range is enormous, and the air is thin enough that even a short walk makes you breathe hard. Chandra Taal, a lake shaped like a crescent moon, is a short and rough detour from the road near the pass, and is one of the high points of any trip in this region.

The riding is demanding rather than technical. On the Lahaul side, the road climbs in a series of hairpins on a surface that varies from broken tarmac to loose stone, with streams that run across it and can be deep in the afternoon when the snow melts. The descent toward Losar is broad and bumpy. Landslides and stalled trucks can hold things up. Altitude sickness is a real risk if you have come up fast, so take a day to acclimatise, drink water and be willing to turn back.

Kaza, in Spiti, and Keylong or Tandi, on the Lahaul side, are where to fill up, and it is sensible to carry a reserve. Start early, because the water crossings are easier in the morning, and keep an eye on the weather.
t.lamayuru@34.3,76.8:
Lamayuru looks like another planet, and the people who named the surrounding hills Moonland were not exaggerating. Wind and water have carved the pale clay slopes into a maze of ridges and spires, and on top of the largest of them sits the monastery, whitewashed and tangled, with the valley dropping away behind it. A local legend says the valley was once a lake, drained by a saint who made his way through the rock, and the geology lends some support to the idea.

Lamayuru, also called Yuru Kabgyat, is among the oldest and most important monasteries in Ladakh, founded around the tenth or eleventh century and associated with the translator Rinchen Zangpo. It belongs to the Drikung Kagyu school, and monks still follow a full round of prayers. Visitors are welcome in the prayer hall, though you should take off your boots, speak quietly and ask before photographing inside. The annual masked dance festival draws people from across the region, and the village below has a few simple guesthouses and cafes.

The Srinagar to Leh highway reaches Lamayuru after the long climb over the Zoji La and the descent through Dras and Kargil, and the road beyond runs on toward Leh. Between Lamayuru and Khaltse the highway crosses the Fotu La, about 4,100 metres, with a good surface and views of the barren hills, and the road then drops along the Indus valley. The tarmac here is generally decent, but landslides, military convoys and roadworks can add delays, and the weather shifts quickly. The highway is typically open from late spring to autumn.

Fuel is the thing to plan. There are pumps at Kargil and Leh, and the distances between them are long enough that a spare can is sensible, so ask locally about the nearest working pump rather than assuming. At about 3,500 metres, the air is thin, and it is wise to rest for a night before pushing higher. Evenings are cold even in summer, and the sky at night is full of stars.
t.sonamarg@34.3,75.3:
Sonamarg means meadow of gold, and in spring and early summer, when the flowers come out on the grass, the name seems fair. It is a broad, high valley of the Sindh river, at roughly twenty-seven hundred metres, about eighty kilometres north-east of Srinagar on the road to Ladakh, surrounded by snow-streaked peaks, pine forests and glaciers. In winter it is buried in snow, and it was once a stop on the old Silk Road routes that linked Kashmir to Central Asia, with caravans of traders, pilgrims and mules passing through on their way to Leh and beyond.

The ride from Srinagar is a day's pleasure in itself. You leave the Kashmir valley's flat paddy fields, cross the Sindh and follow it upstream through Kangan, where the valley narrows and pines climb the hillsides, and the road rises steadily along the river. The surface is generally paved but can be broken by landslides, water crossings and heavy truck traffic, and military convoys are a regular presence. Take extra care on the narrower stretches, where drivers overtake on blind bends, and be prepared for sudden weather, with rain, hail and low cloud possible at any time of year.

Fuel is the sort of thing that needs planning. Pumps in the mountains are few and sometimes out of stock, so fill up in Srinagar or along the valley before heading up, and carry a small spare if you have a way to do so. The nearest larger town is Pahalgam, though in practice it is on a different valley, and for the Ladakh road you should count on Srinagar and, beyond the pass, Kargil as your main stops. In Sonamarg itself there are simple lodges, tented camps and tea stalls that serve chai, maggi noodles and parathas.

From the town, a walk or pony ride leads to the Thajiwas glacier, a short distance up a side valley, which in summer feeds a cold river and offers close views of a tongue of ice. Further up, the trails to the Vishansar and Krishansar lakes and the Gangabal lake are among the great alpine hikes of Kashmir.

Check conditions before travelling, as security situations, weather and closures can change, and local police and tourist offices have the latest information. The best months are May to September, and the road beyond Sonamarg is closed for much of the winter.
t.zoji la@34.3,75.5:
Zoji La is the door to Ladakh, and it has a reputation to match. At around 3,500 metres, it is the pass that connects the green, wet Kashmir valley with the high, dry country beyond, and the transformation on the far side is startling: one moment you are among pines and flower meadows, the next you are looking at pale, bare mountains, sand-coloured slopes and a sky of unbroken blue. The reason is simple. The Himalaya catches the monsoon on one side and leaves the other in a rain shadow, so you cross not only a pass but a climate boundary.

The road up from Baltal is one of the notorious ones. It is narrow, carved into steep slopes with sheer drops on the outer edge, and often no more than a single lane wide in places, with tight hairpins and loose gravel in the corners. Traffic is a mix of army trucks, fuel tankers, buses and bikes, and in busy periods the authorities operate one-way timings, so vehicles go up in one window and down in another. You may find yourself waiting in line for hours, so carry water, food and warm clothes. Rain turns the surface into mud, and landslides can close the road for days.

The pass is generally closed by snow for much of winter, usually opening again in spring once the army has cleared the drifts. A long tunnel has been under construction for years to bypass the worst of it, so check the current situation before you plan your trip. Weather changes rapidly, and even in summer you may encounter snow patches, cold wind and sudden storms.

The first proper town on the far side is Dras, famed as one of the coldest inhabited places in India, and then Kargil. Altitude is another consideration: at this height some riders feel a headache or breathlessness, so take it slowly.

On a clear day, the view back across the valleys is memorable, and the quiet at the top, away from engines, is a reminder that you are standing on a very old route between worlds.
Rajendra Chola I was a king who named his capital after a river trip. After a military campaign that carried his armies as far as the Ganges, he founded a new city about the year 1025 and called it Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the city of the Chola who took the Ganges, and he built a great temple to Shiva at its heart. It stood for two and a half centuries as the capital of one of the great South Indian empires, which at its peak had a navy that reached Southeast Asia. Today the city has gone, but the temple remains, an enormous pyramid of granite rising about fifty-five metres above the surrounding fields, with a tower whose stepped profile is gently curved rather than straight, a style so refined that it feels almost organic.

It belongs to the Great Living Chola Temples, a UNESCO group that includes the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, built by Rajendra's father, and the Airavatesvara at Darasuram. The word living matters: worship still goes on here every day, with priests, flowers, oil lamps and bells, so you share the courtyard with pilgrims, not only visitors. There is an enormous Nandi bull carved from a single block of stone facing the sanctum, and the walls carry fine sculptures of gods and dancers.

The riding is the Kaveri delta at its most generous. This is flat, fertile country, a green quilt of paddy, banana and coconut palms with red-earth roads, temple towers on the horizon and the heat of Tamil Nadu pressing down. The main highways are well surfaced but busy with trucks, buses and autorickshaws, so overtaking needs patience, and the stretches through village centres are full of speed bumps. Summer, from April to June, is brutally hot, so start at first light, and the northeast monsoon from October to December can bring heavy rain and flooding.

The nearest town of any size is Jayamkondam, about nine kilometres away, where you will find petrol stations, shops, small lodges and simple restaurants. Thanjavur and Kumbakonam are larger centres a good distance off. Food in this part of Tamil Nadu centres on rice, sambar, dosas and filter coffee, and the banana leaf meals served at roadside restaurants are good value.

Remember to dress modestly and remove your shoes before entering, and note that the stone courtyard becomes surprisingly hot by midday. Arrive early or late for the best light.
t.lencois@-12.6,-41.4:
Lençóis is the town that the diamond rush built, and it still looks like it. In the 1840s prospectors poured into this corner of Bahia, and the name is said to come from the white tents they pitched along the river, which from the hills looked like sheets laid out to dry. The stone houses along the cobbled lanes are a leftover from that money, painted in faded colours, with a river running clear and tea-brown just below the square, stained by the plants upstream rather than by anything dirty.

You reach it on the BR-242 and the side roads of the Chapada Diamantina, a plateau of sandstone tabletops, canyons and caves in the dry interior of Bahia, a long day from the coast. The riding here is more open than twisty: long, fairly straight asphalt with sudden rises where the plateau steps up, red earth at the verges, scrub that turns green after rain. The Morro do Pai Inácio, the flat-topped rock that this ride is named for, stands a short run away and is worth the climb at sunset, when the whole valley goes amber. Traffic is light apart from trucks, but animals wander onto the road, so keep a little speed in reserve after dark.

Dry season, roughly May to September, is the sensible window for a bike, with clear air and firm gravel on the side tracks. The summer rains can turn the dirt roads to paste and the waterfalls into brown torrents. The town itself is a good base: there are plenty of pousadas, and the evening food runs to river fish, beans and the sweet cassava dishes of the sertão, usually with a cold beer.
