Fuel needs a little planning. Treat Lençóis as your last reliable pump in this stretch, fill the tank before heading south toward Mucugê and Ibicoara, and carry a litre of water. The plateau is wonderful, but the stretches between settlements are long, and the mobile signal comes and goes.
t.mucuge@-13.0,-41.4:
Mucugê has a cemetery that nobody expects. Walk up from the main street and you find the so-called Byzantine cemetery, a field of small white chapel-shaped tombs on a dusty hillside, a legacy of the diamond miners who made this town rich in the nineteenth century and then left it half-empty when the stones ran out. It is a quiet, slightly eerie place at the end of a long day on the road.

The town sits on the southern side of the Chapada Diamantina, in the high plateau country of Bahia. The roads leading in from Lençóis and Ibicoara run through rolling, rocky grassland, with sandstone scarps standing off on either hand and the occasional line of palms in a creek bed. There is very little traffic, and the surface is mostly decent asphalt that has been patched with enthusiasm rather than skill. Watch for potholes at the edges of the villages, for dogs, and for the way a bend can end in a patch of sand blown across the tarmac.

Mucugê is also known for the sempre-vivas, the everlasting flowers that grow on the plateau and were once gathered and sold in bunches. Picking them is now restricted, and the town has a protected park to conserve them, so please photograph rather than pick. On a clear morning the light on the stone and the flowers is as good as anything on the whole loop. The nights are cool for the tropics, since the plateau is well above the lowlands, so a thin jacket is useful even in summer.

This is a small place with no larger town close by. Do not count on finding fuel at any particular hour, and fill up in Lençóis or at the next town you pass before you commit to the stretch. For food, expect modest local restaurants serving rice, beans, manioc and grilled meat, and a cup of strong coffee. The charm of Mucugê is how little it does to be charming: it is a mining town that has quietly become a place to stop.
t.adimali@10.0,77.0:
Adimali is a working town in the cardamom hills of Kerala, on the road that climbs from the plains near Kochi into the high country around Munnar. It is not a tourist town, and nobody comes here for the sights, but it is a handy, lively place, a trading centre for spices, rubber, tea and cardamom, with a crowded bazaar, a lot of buses and the constant beep of horns. It is also the last proper town before the road begins its steepest climb.

The ride up from Kochi is one of the best in the Western Ghats. After Kothamangalam, the road starts to rise, passing through rubber plantations and forests, and then climbing in a long series of bends above the valley of the Periyar river. Two waterfalls, Cheeyappara and Valara, tumble down the cliffs beside the road below Adimali, and in the monsoon they are loud and powerful, spraying mist over the road. The tarmac is generally good, though landslides and heavy rain can cause problems, and the traffic includes heavy lorries, buses and speeding cars.

The landscape changes steadily as you climb. The air gets cooler, the vegetation shifts from tropical forest to cardamom gardens under tall shade trees, and then to the open green of the tea estates. The cardamom hills, a stretch of the Western Ghats, have been planted with spices for generations, and the smell of cardamom and pepper hangs over the roadside stalls. Elephants live in the forests and sometimes cross the road, particularly at dawn and dusk, so be careful on the bends.

Adimali has plenty of fuel stations, shops, and small restaurants serving rice meals, parotta and beef or fish curry, and it is the best place to fill up before the climb. Munnar, about fifteen kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, has more services. The best time to ride is from October to March, when the weather is dry and clear, and in the monsoon, the road can be wet and slippery, with fog, heavy rain and reduced visibility, so take extra care.
t.munnar@10.1,77.1:
Munnar is tea country on a grand scale, a high town in the Western Ghats of Kerala, at about fifteen hundred metres, surrounded by steep green hills that are covered, row on row, in a close-clipped carpet of tea bushes. The slopes are so regular and so bright that they look painted, and the mist moves through them in the morning, turning the valley into a soft, silvery landscape. It is cool here, even when the plains below are baking, and the air has a faint smell of tea leaves.

The tea estates were set up in the late nineteenth century by British planters, who cleared forests and brought in labourers from Tamil Nadu to work the slopes, and the industry still shapes the town. A tea museum shows the old machinery, and the factories around the town can be visited. The hills around Munnar also contain Eravikulam National Park, home of the Nilgiri tahr, a rare mountain goat, and of Anamudi, at 2,695 metres the highest peak in South India. Every twelve years, the slopes around the town turn blue with the flowers of the neelakurinji, a plant that blooms only once in a dozen years, and the next flowering is expected around 2030.

The roads around Munnar are some of the best in Kerala, with winding bends through tea gardens, past waterfalls, lakes and viewpoints. The surface is generally good, though narrow in places, with steep drops and little barrier, and the weather can be wet and foggy, particularly in the monsoon from June to September. The best riding months are from October to March, when the days are clear and cool. Early mornings and late afternoons are the best times for light and for avoiding the heaviest traffic.

Munnar is a busy tourist town with about sixty-eight thousand people in the wider area, and it has fuel stations, shops, hotels and restaurants. The bazaar sells spices, tea, chocolate and local crafts, and there are plenty of places to eat, from simple Kerala meals to Chinese and Indian dishes. It gets crowded during holidays, so book accommodation early, and bring a warm jacket, since the evenings can be chilly.
t.top station@10.1,77.2:
Top Station is the high point of the road between Munnar and the Tamil Nadu border, a viewpoint at about seventeen hundred metres, where the Kerala hills fall away abruptly to the plains of Tamil Nadu far below. The name comes from the days when a ropeway carried tea down from the estates to the railhead at Kottagudi, and this was the topmost station. Today, the ropeway is long gone, but the name has stuck, and the place is a favourite stop for travellers going between Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

The view is the reason to come. From the edge of the plateau, you look out across a huge valley, with the hills of the Western Ghats on one side and the flat, hazy plains of the Theni district on the other, sometimes with a layer of cloud below you. On clear days, the villages and fields of Tamil Nadu are visible far off, and in the late afternoon, the light turns golden. The place is also known for the neelakurinji, which blooms on the slopes in great numbers every twelve years, and the vegetation here is a mix of grassland, shola forest and tea.

The ride from Munnar is a good one, climbing steadily through tea estates, past lakes and viewpoints, with open bends and a smooth surface for much of the way. Fog and rain are common, though, and visibility can drop to a few metres, so ride carefully and use lights. The road continues down the other side toward Bodinayakkanur, with a series of hairpin bends and steep drops, and the temperature rises quickly as you descend.

Munnar is the last reliable stop for fuel on the Kerala side, and Bodinayakkanur, in Tamil Nadu, is the next proper town, about seventeen kilometres away as the crow flies. Bring a jacket and rain cover, since the weather changes fast, and check the border arrangements, as local rules can change.
t.marayoor@10.3,77.2:
Marayoor lies on the dry, rain-shadow side of the Western Ghats, a small town in the Anamalai hills of Kerala where the lush tea country around Munnar gives way to a landscape of sugarcane fields, coconut palms and rocky, scrub-covered hills. It is a different world from the damp green slopes just over the ridge, hotter, drier and quieter, and the change happens within a few kilometres. The people here are mostly farmers, and the pace of life is slow.

Marayoor is known for several things. It has one of the few natural sandalwood forests in India, a protected area where the trees grow wild, and the scent of sandalwood sometimes drifts from the woods. It is also famous for jaggery, the unrefined cane sugar that is made in small workshops around the town, and visitors can watch the cane being crushed and boiled in huge iron pans. In the hills nearby stand ancient dolmens, stone burial chambers built by megalithic people thousands of years ago, which are a quiet reminder of how long the area has been settled.

The ride to Marayoor from Munnar is a fine one, descending from the cool tea hills through a series of curves and forests, with the landscape drying out as you go. The road is generally good, with a few narrow sections, and passes through Chinnar Wildlife Sanctuary, where elephants, deer, and the rare grizzled giant squirrel live. The air becomes warm and dry, and the light is sharper and clearer than on the Munnar side. Watch for animals on the road, particularly in the early morning and at dusk.

Marayoor is a small town with fuel stations, shops and simple restaurants, though the choice is limited compared with Munnar, and the food is mostly local and vegetarian, with rice, sambar and fresh buttermilk. If you are finishing a ride here, it is a pleasant place to stop and rest. Be prepared for the heat, bring water, and try to arrive before dark, since the forest road is a poor place to be after sunset.
t.kalpa@31.5,78.3:
Kalpa is the place where mountains stop being scenery and become an argument. The village sits at about three thousand metres on a ledge above the Sutlej valley in Kinnaur, and directly across the gorge rises Kinner Kailash, a peak of over six thousand metres that Hindus and Buddhists regard as the winter home of Shiva. At sunrise and sunset the snow on its flanks turns pink, then gold, and the effect from the village rooftops is hard to forget. Apple and apricot orchards surround Kalpa, and in autumn the trees are loaded with fruit.

The road that brings you here is the old Hindustan-Tibet road, which follows the Sutlej upstream through a dramatic gorge, hugging cliffs, crossing landslides and passing through hamlets of timber and slate. It is a serious mountain road: narrow, often broken by rockfalls, and in the monsoon, from July to September, it can be closed for days at a time. Early starts help, because the afternoon brings cloud and rain, and small stones fall from above without warning. Keep your speed down and your eyes on the cliff as well as the surface.

Recong Peo, just below Kalpa, is the district headquarters and the place to stock up on fuel and supplies. Above this point, the road toward Spiti goes through remote country, where petrol pumps are few and far between, so fill the tank here and carry spare if you can. Kalpa itself has guesthouses, a monastery and a small market. Local food includes dishes of rice, lentils and mountain greens, with apple products such as juice and jam.

The old part of Kalpa has temples with carved wooden doors and a mix of Hindu and Buddhist traditions, reflecting the crossroads at which Kinnaur stands. Take time to adapt to the altitude, since three thousand metres is enough to cause headaches, and drink plenty of water. Come between May and October for the best weather. The road onward into Spiti climbs into a bare and wide land, a different world from these green slopes.
t.tanglang la@33.5,77.8:
At 5,328 metres, Tanglang La is among the highest motorable passes in the world, and for many riders it is the day when the Himalaya stops being a postcard. It is the second-highest pass on the Manali-Leh Highway, after you have crossed Baralacha La and Lachulung La, and it marks the line between the high plateau of Rupshu and the Indus valley beyond. The air carries about half the oxygen of sea level, so even a short walk will leave you breathless, and the engine of your bike will feel the difference too.

The road approaches through the More Plains, a high, flat desert of gravel and sand at about 4,700 metres, with distant snow peaks and a feeling of enormous emptiness. After the plains, it starts to climb in long, easy switchbacks, past Pang, a tent camp at the start of the ascent, and finally reaches the top, marked by a signboard and a pile of prayer flags. Beyond, the descent to Upshi and the Indus is long and fast, with the land turning from bare rock to the first green of Ladakh's villages.

This is serious country. Altitude sickness is a real risk, and the safest approach is to spend time at lower stops, to ride only a short time at the top and to drink plenty of water. Weather changes quickly, with snow possible even in summer and strong, cold winds on the pass. The road is paved in places but broken in others, with stream crossings fed by melting snow that can be deep and fast in the afternoon. The pass is normally open from about June to early autumn.

The last pump before a long stretch is at Tandi, on the Manali side, so fill up there and carry spare in cans, while the next dependable stations are near Leh. Food at the tented camps is basic, with noodles, rice and tea. Ride in the morning, when the streams are lowest and the weather is steadiest, and give yourself time to rest. A cup of hot tea at the top, with the prayer flags snapping in the wind, is a small reward.
t.great himalayan national park conservati:
The Great Himalayan National Park is a long name for a wild place. It lies in the Kullu district of Himachal Pradesh, at the meeting of several river valleys, the Tirthan, the Sainj and the Jiwa Nal, and it protects a steep forested wilderness that climbs from about fifteen hundred metres to over six thousand. It was established in the 1980s and listed by UNESCO in 2014, for its extraordinary biodiversity. Snow leopards, Himalayan tahr, brown bears and musk deer live here, and the forests are home to the western tragopan, a pheasant with a brilliant red and spotted plumage, and the monal, whose feathers shine in the sun like metal.

The park is mostly roadless, which is the point. Treks go on foot from villages such as those in the Tirthan valley, and local guides and homestays are the way in. The Tirthan is a clear trout stream, and its villages, with their wooden houses, apple orchards and prayer flags, are a quiet alternative to the busy resorts of Manali.

The ride that comes here starts in Shimla and takes a long day. The road descends from the ridge, passes Narkanda and then cuts south of the Sutlej toward Aut and Banjar, while the Jalori Pass, at over three thousand metres, offers a quiet link across the range, with pine, spruce and meadow on its slopes. The roads are narrow and in places rough, with landslides common in the monsoon between July and September. In winter, snow can close the high sections.

Banjar is the last sizeable settlement, and fuel and supplies are limited beyond it, so fill up earlier and carry spare. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the skies are clear and the forests are bright with rhododendron or turning leaves. Be patient on the road, give trucks space on the bends and expect delays. Buy local honey and dried fruit, and sleep in a homestay, where the food is cooked on a wood fire, and the night sky is filled with stars.
t.kalka shimla railway@30.9,76.9:
The Kalka–Shimla Railway is a two-foot-six-inch narrow gauge line that climbs about ninety-six kilometres from the plains at Kalka to Shimla, the old summer capital of British India. It opened in 1903, was built to carry officials and their luggage up to the hills away from the heat, and it does the job by means of an extraordinary number of tunnels, around a hundred, plus hundreds of bridges and arched viaducts. The longest tunnel, at Barog, is more than a kilometre long, and the story of the engineer who miscalculated the alignment and was fined a rupee is a local legend. UNESCO added the line to the World Heritage List in 2008.

Kalka itself is a busy small town at the foot of the Shivalik hills, and the railway station is the place where the toy train, as everyone calls it, waits at its platform in blue and cream, with a small engine. Parwanoo and Kasauli, close by, are hill stations in their own right, Kasauli with its old cantonment, its church and its quiet pine forests. Behind it all the Himalayan foothills begin, and the air cools quickly as you rise.

The road to Shimla follows the same route, NH5 through Parwanoo and Solan, and in recent years it has been widened, with long tunnels and cuts through the hills. The riding is a grind of hairpins, with heavy truck traffic and buses, though it can be rewarding to watch the toy train cross a viaduct beside the road. Monsoon landslides regularly close parts of it, and in July and August heavy rain has destroyed sections, so check conditions. In winter, black ice and snow appear above Solan, and in the evenings fog rolls in.

There is no shortage of services, with fuel stations in Kalka, Parwanoo and all along the highway, and dhabas that serve parathas, dal and sweet tea to truckers and tourists. Kalka is a good place to fill up, because climbing is thirsty work for an engine, and the bike will appreciate the break. If you can, time your ride to coincide with a train departure, and watch the little locomotive gather itself and puff out of the station.
t.mankulam range@10.4,77.2:
The Mankulam range lies in the high country of Idukki district in Kerala, in the Munnar uplands that form the highest part of the Western Ghats south of the Nilgiris. The mountains here are enormous, rolling green downs of grass dotted with dark patches of shola, the stunted evergreen forest that fills the folds between the ridges, and the entire landscape is part of a protected block that includes Anamudi, at 2,695 metres the highest peak in India south of the Himalaya. The Grass Hills National Park sits here, with its sweeping slopes and strange, windswept look.

Nilgiri tahr, a stocky mountain goat, graze on the cliffs, and in the sholas live elephants, sambar and the rare Nilgiri marten. The best-known botanical event in the region is the flowering of the neelakurinji, a shrub whose blue blooms cover the hills once in twelve years; the last great flowering was in 2018, so the next will not come until about 2030. At lower elevations, the sandalwood forests near Marayur are unusual in Kerala, and the region has a collection of megalithic burial dolmens that go back thousands of years.

The road in from Kochi is a long day, but a rewarding one. The national highway climbs from the coastal plains through rubber and teak, past waterfalls, then up a long series of hairpins into tea country around Munnar, where the slopes are combed with perfectly even rows of bushes. Beyond Munnar the road runs on toward Marayur, dropping into a drier valley with sugarcane and jaggery boilers. The surface is generally good, but buses and tourist jeeps clog the road at weekends, and fog is common above 1,500 metres. Carry a jacket, because the temperature can fall to single figures in winter.

Fill up there. The tea stalls sell hot, sweet chai with a slice of bread, and small restaurants serve vegetarian meals on banana leaves. Entry to some forest areas needs a permit, so ask at the Forest Department office, and travel in the dry months from December to March.
t.mannavan shola@10.4,77.2:
Mannavan Shola is a patch of forest in the high hills of Idukki, in the Mankulam forest range, and the word shola is the key to understanding the whole place. In these mountains, the ridges are covered in open grassland, while the folds between them hold dense, dark, evergreen forest, the sholas. They are very old, a relic of colder times, and they trap mist and rainwater, releasing it slowly into the streams. The grassy hillsides and the sholas work as a single system, and it is the reason this part of the Western Ghats is so important as a source of water for southern India.

The air is cool and often wet, and the forest floor is thick with moss, ferns and wild orchids, with trees hung with lichen. In the sholas live Nilgiri tahr, the Nilgiri langur and elusive predators like the leopard, and birds such as the Nilgiri pipit, which is found nowhere else, sing out of the grass. In the clear evening light, the colours are astonishing, with amber grass and blue mountains lined up in rows to the horizon.

For a rider, the roads here are some of the finest in the south, though demanding. The route from Kochi to Munnar and Marayur climbs steadily to cool altitudes, passing waterfalls and tea gardens, and beyond Munnar the road turns into a lonely stretch of curves and sudden views. Fog is common, and in heavy rain visibility can drop to a few metres, so keep your lights on and your speed low. The surface varies, with fresh asphalt in places and broken edges in others.

There are no services at the shola itself, and you should reckon on Marayur, about twelve kilometres away, as the nearest place for tea, snacks and basic supplies, with Munnar being the better choice for fuel. Entry to the protected areas is regulated, so ask first, and respect the rules about staying on the road and not leaving rubbish. If you can, arrive early on a weekday, when the mist is still in the valleys, and wait a while for the sun to burn it off.
t.leh manali highway point 2@32.4,77.2:
Sissu is the first village on the far side of the Atal Tunnel, and the landscape changes at once. In Manali the hills are green and wooded, but here in the upper Chandra valley of Lahaul, the monsoon barely reaches, and the mountains are bare, brown and grey, with glaciers hanging on the heights. The village sits at about three thousand metres beside the river, with a waterfall that tumbles down the cliff, and poplar and willow trees along the stream. Manali is sixteen kilometres or so behind, and Kyelang, the district town, lies further north.

Riding out of the tunnel is a strange experience. After nine kilometres in the dark, you emerge into bright sun and a different world, with a wide valley and snowy peaks. The road to Keylong is good, a smooth ribbon of tarmac along the river, with long bends and views of the Lahaul mountains. Be careful of sudden changes in weather, and of gravel and meltwater across the road where streams come down from the slopes. The altitude here is enough to make some riders feel a little breathless.

Lahaul is a land of Buddhist monasteries and villages with flat-roofed houses and prayer flags, where the culture is closer to Tibet than to the plains of India. The people grow barley, peas and potatoes in the short summer. The mountains here are crowned with ice, and the river that runs beside the road, the Chandra, is a milky grey from the glacier water. Marmots and mountain birds live on the higher slopes.

Fuel is not sold in Sissu itself, so make sure you have filled up in Manali, and plan to refuel at Tandi, the last pump before Leh. A few dhabas and guesthouses serve travellers, and the food is simple but hot. The road is usually open from about May or June to October, though the tunnel makes it accessible earlier than before. The weather can be cold, and rain or snow can come at any time, so pack warm and waterproof clothes.
t.leh manali highway point 3@32.7,77.4:
Baralacha La is a pass at about 4,850 metres, a bare, wind-blasted saddle where the road crosses between Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh, and the landscape feels like the edge of the world. Near the top lies Suraj Tal, a high, round lake that reflects the sky, and the mountains around are snow-capped even in summer. Three rivers, the Chandra, the Bhaga and the Yunam, rise in this area and flow in different directions. Kyelang lies a long way back, some forty kilometres by the crow, and there is nothing else near.

The road to the pass is a long, steady climb, and the surface can be rough, with patches of gravel, potholes and water crossings from the melting snow. The air is thin, and the engine of the bike loses power, so take it gently. At this altitude, altitude sickness is a danger, with headaches, nausea and breathlessness, and it is wise to ascend slowly and carry water. The wind is bitter, and gloves and a windproof jacket are essential. The views, though, are stunning, with the lake, the glaciers and the endless ridges.

The landscape is high-altitude desert, with little vegetation apart from tufts of grass and tiny flowers. Wildlife is sparse, but you may see marmots, Himalayan snowcocks and, with luck, blue sheep on the higher slopes. Shepherds bring their flocks to the high pastures in summer, and you may meet them with their sheep and goats on the road. The nights are freezing even in July, and snow can fall in any month.

Fill up at Tandi before the climb, and carry spare fuel if you can. The road is open only from about June to October, and the pass can be blocked by snow even then. Check the road status with local sources, and be prepared for delays. A tent camp at Zing Zing Bar, on the way, offers a bed for those who need a rest.
t.leh manali highway point 4@32.9,77.6:
Sarchu is a place with no village, only tents. At about 4,300 metres, on the high plateau between the Himachal and Ladakh borders, a scatter of seasonal camps sits beside a stream, serving as an overnight halt for riders and drivers on the long road to Leh. The nearest settlements are far away, and the landscape is a vast bowl of brown hills, with snow peaks on the horizon and a sky that seems enormous. The mountains are bare, and the air is thin and cold.

The ride north from Sarchu begins with the Gata Loops, a series of twenty-one hairpin bends that climb the slope in a tight zigzag, and goes on over the Nakee La and Lachulung La passes. The road is a mix of tarmac and rough gravel, with sections washed out by streams, and the going is slow. The altitude is a challenge, with a risk of headaches and sleeplessness for those who have not acclimatised. A night at Sarchu is a test, and many riders prefer to descend to a lower camp to sleep.

The tent camps offer basic beds, hot meals and tea, and they are the only shelter for many kilometres. They operate only in summer, and the facilities are simple, with shared toilets and sometimes no electricity. The food is dal, rice and noodles. The stars at night are astonishing, with the Milky Way a bright band across the sky, and the cold is intense, so a thick sleeping bag is a good idea.

The road is open from about June to September, and the weather can turn quickly, with snow and wind. If you are feeling unwell with altitude symptoms, descend immediately. The border between Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh is here, and the road continues north toward Pang and the More Plains.
t.leh manali highway point 5@33.1,77.7:
Pang is a cluster of tents at about 4,500 metres, perched at the foot of a series of hairpins on the Leh-Manali Highway, and it is the last stop before the road climbs onto the high plateau. The settlement consists of a few dhabas and tent camps serving the passing traffic in summer, and it has a rough, frontier feel. A short way beyond lies the Moray Plains, a vast flat expanse at about 4,700 metres, where the road runs straight for kilometres across a gravel desert surrounded by distant mountains.

The ride on the plains is a surreal experience. After the climb up the hairpins, the road becomes a straight, level ribbon, with a surface of tarmac in fair condition and a wide view in all directions. The wind blows hard, and dust devils spin across the plain. Having crossed the Lachulung La, at over 5,000 metres, before Pang, the road goes on to the Tanglang La, at about 5,300 metres, one of the highest motorable passes in the world. The air is thin, and the bike will feel sluggish.

The landscape is a high-altitude desert, with no trees and few plants, but the colours of the rock are striking: red, ochre and grey. The Moray Plains are home to the kiang, the wild ass of the Tibetan plateau, which you may see grazing in small herds. Nomadic herders, the Changpa, bring their sheep and pashmina goats to these pastures in summer. The nights are bitterly cold, and the days are bright and dry.

Fuel is not available at Pang, so make sure you fill up in advance and carry spare. The tents offer basic food and a place to sleep, but the altitude can make the night uncomfortable. The road is open from about June to September, and a sudden snowstorm can cut it at any time. Carry warm clothing, water and food, and check the road conditions before you set off. If you feel dizzy or sick, descend to a lower altitude.
t.leh manali highway point 6@33.2,77.8:
Somewhere past the loops that drop off Tanglang La, the mountains step back and the road runs out onto a wide, pale plateau. The air is thin enough that a bike loses a visible slice of its power, and a rider who climbed out of Leh a few hours ago can feel a dull pressure behind the eyes if the day started too fast. Go slowly and drink more water than seems sensible.

The riding here is odd, and I mean that kindly. After days of hairpins the tarmac simply goes straight for kilometres between dun-coloured ridges, with the sky doing all the work. Surface is mostly good but patched, with frost heave, sand drifts and the occasional stream washing across in the afternoon when the snowmelt picks up. Wind is the real opponent. It comes down the plain in gusts that can shove a loaded bike across a lane, so keep your lines wide and your grip loose.

This is nomad country. Changpa herders bring pashmina goats and sheep to these pastures, and in summer you may see their dark tents beside a stream, with a few yaks and a scatter of dogs. Kiang, the wild ass of the Tibetan plateau, sometimes stand in the distance and watch you pass with complete disinterest. There are marmots near the roadside burrows on lower slopes and the light at midday is hard and white, so dark glasses are not optional.

Nothing here sells fuel, and the ordinary rule on this highway is to treat each tank as the only one you will get. Leh is the last dependable pump to the north, and riders going the other way know the one at Tandi in Himachal as the long-awaited relief before the big stretch. Carry a spare can. Tea and noodles are available at seasonal tented camps along this belt, and in the main season there are guesthouses at Pang and Sarchu where you can drop your altitude a little and sleep. Do not push on after dark: road signs are few, the cold at night is severe, and a breakdown out here is a long wait.

The highway is open only in the warmer months, usually from about June until the first big snows of autumn, and the exact dates swing with the winter. Check before you set out and expect delays for convoys or slides on any day.
t.manali leh highway point 3@33.0,77.6:
Sarchu is not a village so much as a seasonal camp in a broad, windy basin at roughly 4,300 metres, where Himachal Pradesh gives way to Ladakh. There is nothing permanent here: a collection of tented camps and a couple of rough dhabas serve riders and truck drivers in summer, then pack up when the snow comes. The setting is vast and treeless, with colossal bare mountains in rose and ochre and a river running through the gravel. The air is thin and the cold at night is serious, so many travellers feel the altitude strongly.

The road here has become something of a legend. From the south it climbs over Baralacha La, a pass of nearly 4,900 metres, and then drops to the plain where Sarchu sits. North of the camps it tackles the Gata Loops, a series of twenty-one hairpins that climb the mountainside like a stack of paper clips, followed by the high passes of Nakee La and Lachulung La. Surface conditions vary hugely. In some years there is fresh asphalt; in others there are water crossings, loose rock and washed-out edges, and the road can be closed for hours by landslides or meltwater.

Fuel is not available in any practical way. Keylong is far behind and the next dependable supply lies well beyond the plateau, so carry what you need, and carry a basic tool kit. Heavy rain is rare, but sudden snow flurries can arrive in any month. Altitude sickness is a real danger, and the standard advice is to drink water, go slowly, and descend if headaches become severe.

The tented camps serve dal, rice and noodles, and a warm blanket and a mug of tea are worth a great deal. If you sleep here, bring a proper sleeping bag, and expect a night sky of amazing clarity. In the morning, the frost on the bike seat will tell you what you slept through.
t.manali leh highway point 4@33.1,77.8:
There is a sort of bleakness in this stretch of road that gets under the skin. Pang is a collection of tents and tea stalls rather than a village, and around it the earth turns the colour of rust and bone. Everything here is open to the sky, and the weather can switch from sunshine to snow in an hour.

The riding is demanding in a way that has nothing to do with traffic. The road climbs in long, steep stretches over passes such as Lachulung La and then spreads out across the flat, wind-scoured plain known as the More Plains, a dead-straight run of tens of kilometres with mirages shimmering ahead. The surface can be good tarmac one moment and torn gravel the next, and streams cross the road after warm afternoons. Wind in the open plain can be punishing, and the thin air makes engines run weak, so expect your bike to lose power and take things gently.

This is the Changthang edge, the high country that stretches east toward Tibet. Nomadic herders, the Changpa, move their pashmina goats and yaks across the plateau, living in black yak-hair tents in summer. Wild asses, the kiang, are sometimes seen grazing on the plains, and marmots whistle from burrows along the roadside. The geology is spectacular, with folded layers of sedimentary rock lifted high and carved by wind.

Practicalities are minimal. Fuel is not on offer, so you rely on what you carry from Keylong or Tandi, and water is best bought in sealed bottles. Tea stalls serve noodles and omelettes, and the simple meal tastes better than anywhere. Temperatures at night fall well below freezing even in summer, and the daytime sun burns the skin at this altitude, so cover up. Leave early and arrive early, and keep a close eye on the sky.
t.manali leh highway point 5@33.5,77.8:
Tanglang La is one of the highest motorable passes on the planet, at roughly 5,300 metres, and the signboard at the top proudly claims second place in the world. Whatever the official ranking, the air here holds about half the oxygen that you breathe at sea level, and a few minutes of walking leaves you gasping. Prayer flags snap in the wind, a small shrine marks the summit, and the surrounding peaks are bare and pale. Nobody stays long; photographs are taken at speed, and the engine struggles when you ride away.

The approach from the south crosses the desert plateau and then climbs by long, steady gradients and a handful of hairpins to the summit. The road surface varies from adequate to rough, with sections that are often broken by meltwater. On the northern side the descent is long and relatively smooth, losing altitude steadily down into the Rumtse valley and toward the Indus. The cold is fierce even in July, wind-chill can freeze fingers inside gloves, and sudden storms can bring snow and zero visibility.

The whole region sits in a rain shadow, so the landscape is a desert of rock, gravel and bare slopes with almost no vegetation. At lower altitude on the northern side, the first signs of human life appear again: stone walls, patches of barley and the white chortens of Buddhist villages such as Rumtse, which marks the starting point of a famous trek to the lake of Tso Moriri. Wildlife is rare at the summit but Himalayan marmots and wild asses live in the plains below.

There are no services here, so fuel and food must come from earlier on the route. The nearest settlements are small, and the nearest big town, Leh, lies about a hundred kilometres ahead. Take a few minutes at the top to breathe slowly, drink some water, and enjoy the sense of having reached the roof of the road, then head down gently, because a rider with a headache and a tired bike belongs at lower altitude.
t.srinagar leh highway point 2@34.3,75.3:
Sonamarg means the meadow of gold, and in early summer the grass here is a bright, flower-flecked green with the glaciers of the main Himalaya shining behind it. The Sindh river runs milky and fast through the middle of the valley, and fir and birch forests climb the slopes to the snowline. At about 2,700 metres, it is cool and clear, and this is where most travellers feel the road to Ladakh has really begun. Pahalgam is the nearest sizeable town, but that is in another valley, so for services you rely on what you find in the small bazaar here and on the road out of Srinagar.

Sonamarg was long a staging post on the old caravan route between Kashmir and Ladakh, where traders from Yarkand and Tibet rested before crossing the Zoji La. Today it is a popular summer destination for Indian visitors, with ponies and day-trippers heading for the Thajiwas glacier, an easy trek from the meadow. Trout swim in the river, and Gujjar and Bakarwal herders bring their sheep and goats up to the high pastures in summer, living in simple huts and tents.

The road in is a pleasant, rising ride alongside the river. Corners are moderate, the surface is generally good, and the scenery is beautiful. Traffic, however, can be a problem. Army convoys, trucks and tourist vehicles can build up long queues, and overtaking requires patience and care. Landslides and shooting stones can close the road after rain, so keep an eye on the cliffs above.

Fuel is available at stations on the approach, but supplies at Sonamarg itself can be limited, so fill your tank earlier. The bazaar has snack stalls with fried bread, tea and omelettes. Mornings are the best time to ride, when the road is clear and the light on the peaks is bright. Bring a waterproof, because rain showers come quickly, and a warm layer for the pass ahead.
t.srinagar leh highway point 3@34.3,75.5:
Zoji La is the gateway between Kashmir and Ladakh, a pass at about 3,500 metres where the green, wet world of the valley gives way abruptly to the dry, brown, empty land beyond. The climb from Sonamarg is steep and exposed, the road cut into the mountainside above the Sindh river gorge, with huge drops and narrow lanes. In many places the road is barely wide enough for two vehicles, and the surface can be rough, wet and muddy. This is regularly cited as one of the most dangerous roads in India, and the reputation is earned.

Traffic on the pass is controlled by timings, with one-way windows for vehicles going each direction, and the system exists because the road is too narrow for safe passing. Check the schedule before setting out. Heavy lorries, military convoys and buses grind upward in low gear, and queues can be long. Snow can close the pass from late autumn into spring, and avalanches have swept the road in the past. A long tunnel beneath the pass has been under construction for years, intended to give year-round access, but at the time of writing the old road is the main route.

The change on the other side is dramatic. Crossing the summit, you leave behind the pine and the meadow flowers, and the valley opens out into the rainshadow desert of Ladakh. Within a few kilometres the trees vanish, the hills turn the colour of dry biscuit, and the wind begins to blow. The air feels thinner and sharper.

Carry water and a warm jacket, because the weather here can change within minutes. Mornings are better, with less traffic and clearer skies. Patience is the key virtue. The road has been used for centuries by traders, soldiers and pilgrims, and every one of them has stories of mud, cold and delay. Take it slowly, and keep a safe distance from the lorry in front.
t.srinagar leh highway point 4@34.4,75.8:
Drass is known as one of the coldest inhabited places in the world, and the winter temperatures here, which have fallen close to minus forty-five Celsius, justify the reputation. The small town lies at roughly 3,300 metres in a wide, treeless valley beyond the Zoji La, with snow-covered peaks all around. In summer the climate is cool and dry, with strong sun and a hard blue sky, and the barley fields turn gold in late summer. The villages are built of stone and mud brick, with flat roofs where hay is stacked for winter.

Drass is also a place of memory. In 1999 the Kargil conflict between India and Pakistan was fought on the heights above the road, and the Kargil War Memorial, built in honour of the Indian soldiers who fell, stands beside the highway. It has a museum, a wall of names and a flag, and the nearby peaks, including Tololing, are pointed out by guides. Visitors are asked to be quiet and respectful. The highway here ran in the line of fire, which is why the area is heavily patrolled.

The population is mostly of Dard ancestry, with Shina-language speakers and a long history of trading and herding. Many families keep sheep and goats, and in the early morning you may see herds on the road. The ride through here is straightforward, with a good surface and long, open stretches of tarmac, and the landscape is bare and grand. Wind can be strong in the afternoon. Cold at night is serious even in summer.

Services are modest. There are small dhabas selling tea and noodles, and a fuel station in the area, though it is wise to check before relying on it. The larger town of Kargil lies about sixty kilometres ahead, and it has more choice. Stop at the memorial if you can, and stay for a hot tea.
t.srinagar leh highway point 6@34.3,76.9:
Few stretches of road in Ladakh change as sharply as the descent from the Fotu La to the Indus. This is the highest point on the Srinagar-Leh highway, at around 4,100 metres, marked by prayer flags and a cairn, and from there the road drops in broad bends into the valley of the great river near the village of Khalsi. Below the pass, the first apricot trees and the fields of barley appear, and suddenly there is water, green and loud, running down from the snows. After the dry heights, the contrast is a pleasure.

The road at this point is among the most enjoyable of the whole journey. The tarmac is generally good, the curves are open, and the long, bare ridges offer views down into the valley. Rock walls rise on both sides, and the road snakes between sandy hillsides carved by wind and water. Surface quality can deteriorate after rain or rockfall, so keep alert for gravel on corners. Traffic includes army trucks and tourist vehicles, and drivers often cut across bends, so keep to the left of your lane.

Khalsi lies at the point where the road meets the Indus, and from here the highway follows the river most of the way to Leh. It is a small village, with a bridge across the river and a few shops and tea stalls. Nearby, old inscriptions cut into the rock hint at how long this river corridor has carried people between Kashmir, Tibet and the plains, long before the tarmac arrived.

Fuel is not reliably available around here, so keep the tank topped up from Kargil or Leh. The weather is generally dry, and afternoons can be hot at this lower altitude, with the sun reflecting off the pale rock. Try to start early in the morning. Mornings are calm, the road is quiet, and the first light on the hills brings out the warm browns and pinks.
t.srinagar leh highway point 7@34.3,76.8:
Lamayuru looks like the Moon with a monastery stuck on top, and that is not much of an exaggeration. The gompa perches on a ridge of eroded, pale clay and sandstone above a cluster of whitewashed houses, with a landscape of ridges, gullies and crumbling pinnacles falling away on either side. Local legend says the valley was once a lake, drained by a saint who opened a gap in the mountains so that people could settle, and geologists confirm that it really was a lake bed, now carved into the strange formations known as Moonland.

The monastery is among the oldest and most important in Ladakh, with roots said to reach back to the tenth or eleventh century and to the translator Rinchen Zangpo, though the buildings you see have been rebuilt many times. It belongs to the Drikung Kagyu school, and the main hall contains painted walls and statues. Monks are often seen on the roof, and a small guesthouse and a few cafés near the gate serve tea, noodles and thukpa. Each year, in summer, a masked dance festival draws crowds in from the surrounding villages.

On the road, you are well along the Srinagar-Leh highway, in a region where the highway curls between bare mountains and tight valleys. The riding is a joy: broad, easy bends climb to the Namika La and Fotu La passes, with good views, a decent surface and a fine feeling of space. The ground is dry and brittle, so rockfall is possible, and a sudden afternoon wind can throw sand across the tarmac. Overtaking army convoys and lorries needs care, since sight lines are short on some bends.

Services are limited; the village has simple guesthouses and homestays, but fuel is a matter for planning, with Kargil behind you and Leh ahead. At about 3,500 metres, the air is thin, so walk slowly and drink water. The light is best in the early morning and the late afternoon, when shadows deepen across the ridges and the monastery glows gold.
t.spiti circuit point 2@31.5,78.3:
Reckong Peo is the district headquarters of Kinnaur, a place of tight hairpins, cliff-hung roads, and views of one of the finest mountains in the Himalayan foothills. Across the Sutlej valley, the peaks of Kinner Kailash rise to over 6,000 metres, and when the sun hits the summit at dawn, the rock glows red. At around 2,700 metres, Peo is an administrative town, busy with government offices, shops and a market, but a short ride above it lies Kalpa, a quieter village famed for its apple orchards and its view of the mountain.

This part of the Spiti circuit follows the old Hindustan-Tibet Road, a highway that clings to the cliff, in places carved from the rock itself. The surface is usually good, but landslides, falling rocks and sudden road washouts are common during the monsoon, and some sections have notorious overhangs. The valley is narrow and deep, with the Sutlej river thundering far below, and traffic includes buses, lorries and trucks carrying apples.

Kinnaur has a distinct culture, a blend of Hindu and Buddhist traditions that is reflected in its wooden temples with carved doors, its green felt caps worn by older men, and its fruit. The apple harvest in autumn is the main activity, and stalls along the road offer baskets of fruit. Local wine and the strong spirit called chulli, made from apricots, are part of village life. In the old temple at Kalpa, carved wood and slate roofs recall the style found in Tibet.

Services are good here, with fuel, a bank and basic repair shops, but supplies grow thin beyond. Fill up, buy snacks, and get an early night, because the days ahead include some of the most demanding riding on the circuit. Weather is mild in the day and cool in the evening. The best time to ride is from May to October.
t.spiti circuit point 3@31.9,78.6:
Nako is a village on a ledge above a little lake, a cluster of flat-roofed stone houses at about 3,600 metres in the upper Hangrang valley, just where Kinnaur begins to turn into Spiti. The lake sits in a cup of the hillside, ringed by willow and poplar trees, and in winter it freezes solid and people skate on it. Beyond the village, the mountains are bare, brown and enormous, and the air feels clean and thin. You are crossing a frontier here between the green, wet Himalaya of the south and the cold, dry plateau of the north.

The village has a small collection of ancient temples, which are said to have been founded by the great translator Rinchen Zangpo around the turn of the first millennium, and they hold clay statues and painted walls whose colours remain deep. Visits are usually possible by asking at the village, and the caretaker may take you inside. Footprints of a saint are shown on a stone near the lake, and prayer wheels line a path near the houses.

The road to Nako climbs in long, steep switchbacks from the Sutlej gorge, in a series of hairpins that rise past the village of Pooh. It is a narrow road with long drops and rough sections, and the surface is often broken by rockfall. Sudden weather changes can bring rain or snow, and the road can be closed for several days by landslides or heavy snow, so keep your schedule flexible.

Homestays and small guesthouses provide basic meals of dal, rice and thick bread, and the pace of life is slow. Altitude can bring headaches, so rest, drink water and walk gently. The light on the lake in the early morning, with the peaks reflected, is worth getting up for.
t.spiti circuit point 4@32.2,78.1:
Kaza is the administrative centre of Spiti, a town of low buildings spread across a broad plain beside the Spiti river at about 3,800 metres. The landscape around it is staggering, a desert of pale rock, deep gorges and bare mountains, with a few green patches of barley and peas where villagers have brought water down from the snow. Tibetan culture runs deep here, and the name Spiti means the middle land, a reference to its position between India and Tibet.

Kaza is the largest place for a long way, so you can rely on finding fuel, a bank, small hotels, simple restaurants and workshops, although supplies sometimes run short in the busy season. The pump is a vital fixture for anyone riding the circuit, and queues can form. A Buddhist monastery sits above the town, and the famous Key Gompa lies a short ride away, a stack of mud-brick buildings piled on a hilltop, with a tradition going back about a thousand years. Painted walls, butter lamps and the sound of horns and cymbals fill the prayer hall, and young monks study here.

The valley is also known for its high villages, including Kibber and Langza, where fossil seashells can be found in the rocks, a reminder that this land was once a seabed, lifted up by the collision of India with Asia. Snow leopards live in the surrounding mountains, and wildlife tours in winter draw visitors, though sightings are rare. Ibex are easier to spot.

The roads around Kaza are the real attraction, wide valley tracks with mountain views, but also steep climbs to remote villages on gravel and rock. Surfaces vary, and water crossings appear after warm afternoons. The weather is dry and bright but cold, and the wind can be fierce. Temperatures at night are often below freezing. Try thukpa, momos and butter tea in the town, and look for the small bakeries that cater to travellers.

Kunzum La is a pass that most riders approach with a mix of excitement and fatigue, a rocky saddle at about 4,500 metres that separates Spiti from Lahaul. At the top, a small shrine decorated with prayer flags, yak horns and offerings stands beside the road, and riders traditionally circle it once, clockwise, and honk a horn for luck. The view takes in a sea of snow peaks, glaciers that tumble from the heights, and the vast empty valleys on both sides.

The road to the pass climbs from the Spiti valley in a series of broad hairpins, with a surface that ranges from decent to terrible. In dry weather it is a rocky track with loose gravel and ruts, and after rain or snow it can become a slippery mess. Water crossings appear in the afternoons, and the weather can turn quickly, with cloud and snow flurries even in midsummer. The descent on the Lahaul side is long and steep, passing below the glacier fields and following the Chandra river toward the Rohtang road.

The pass is closed by snow from about late October until early summer, and it usually opens when the army clears the road. Do not attempt to cross it without checking conditions locally. A short, rough side track leads to Chandra Tal, the Moon Lake, a stunning blue lake in a bowl of mountains, which many riders visit on foot or on a quick detour. The glacier-fed lake is a sacred site and a popular campsite, and it is wise to treat it with care.

There are no services at the pass. Fuel must be carried from Kaza, and food and water too. The nearest tea stalls are found at the bottom of the Lahaul side, and they offer noodles and tea in tents. The altitude is high enough to cause headaches, so ride slowly, rest, and drink water. A quiet moment at the shrine, with the wind in the flags, is a good way to remember why you came.
t.near manali@32.2,77.2:
Apple orchards, deodar cedars and the roar of the Beas river surround Manāli, the hill town at the head of the Kullu Valley in Himachal Pradesh, and this spot lies just outside it, at the point where the road to Ladakh starts its long climb into the high Himalaya. Manāli sits at about two thousand metres, and from here the snow peaks of the Pir Panjal range rise straight up behind the town, with the Rohtang Pass hidden above.

Manāli has a long history as a trading and pilgrimage centre, and the old wooden Hadimba Devi temple, set in a cedar forest above the town, dates from the sixteenth century and is dedicated to a local goddess from the Mahabharata. In nearby Vashisht, hot springs feed public baths beside an old temple, and across the river, Old Manāli is a backpacker's village of guesthouses and cafes. The town is busy with Indian tourists all year, especially honeymooners and families escaping the summer heat of the plains, and in winter people come for snow.

For riders, Manāli is the starting point of one of the great motorcycle journeys of the world: the Leh–Manāli Highway, which climbs over a series of high passes to Leh in Ladakh. The first barrier, Rohtang Pass at nearly four thousand metres, used to block the road for much of the year, but the Atal Tunnel, opened in 2020, now runs beneath the Pir Panjal, nearly nine kilometres long, and gives year-round access to the Lahaul valley beyond. The road beyond is long, high and wild, with rough sections, water crossings and altitudes above five thousand metres on passes such as Taglang La.

The riding around Manāli itself is chaotic and steep, with heavy traffic, tour buses, taxis, potholes and landslides in the monsoon. Permits are required to drive up to Rohtang Pass itself, and there are restrictions on the number of vehicles. The road to Leh is generally open from about June to October, depending on snow.

Manāli has fuel, bike rentals, mechanics, food of every kind, and hundreds of hotels. Take time here to acclimatise before going higher, eat well, and check the bike thoroughly: help on the road ahead can be far away.

Leh sits in the high desert of Ladakh at about 3,500 metres, in the broad valley of the Indus, with the Karakoram on one side and the Zanskar range on the other, and it is the end of the Manali-Leh highway, one of the great road journeys in the world. The last stage of that road is the best: you cross the Tanglang La, among the highest passes in the world, then drop to the Indus plain, through villages with whitewashed chortens and prayer flags, and the town appears below a hill crowned by the old Leh Palace, a nine-storey building of mud and wood modelled on the Potala in Lhasa. Behind it, the Namgyal Tsemo monastery and a ruined fort hang on the ridge.

Leh was a major stop on the caravan routes between India, Tibet and Central Asia, where traders brought pashmina, salt, silk and spices over the passes. The Buddhist heritage is strong and visible: the Shanti Stupa, built by Japanese monks, gives a grand view over the town, and monasteries such as Thiksey and Hemis stand within a day's ride, painted with bright murals. The old town below the palace has narrow lanes, and the main bazaar is full of Kashmiri and Tibetan craftwork.

The key to Leh is altitude, and it deserves respect. Spend at least two days there doing nothing before you ride higher, drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol on the first night and take headaches seriously, since acute mountain sickness can become dangerous. The sun is fierce, the air is thin and dry, and the nights are cold even in summer. For riders the roads to Khardung La, to Pangong Lake and to the Nubra Valley all start from here, and some of them need an Inner Line Permit, which can be arranged through a local agency or online. The riding season runs roughly from June to September, when the high roads are open, though landslides and snow can close them at any time.

The town has about thirty-seven thousand people, so fuel, mechanics, tyres and food are all available, but remember that the stations beyond Leh, in the Nubra and Pangong directions, are far apart, so carry a jerrycan for long days. Try thukpa, the noodle soup, momos and butter tea, and the apricots that grow in the valleys. Bakeries sell German-style cakes, a legacy of trekkers, and cafes on the main street have good coffee and views of the palace.

t.near munnar@10.0,77.0:
Munnar is tea country on a grand scale, a high town in the Western Ghats of Kerala, at about fifteen hundred metres, surrounded by steep green hills that are covered, row on row, in a close-clipped carpet of tea bushes. The slopes are so regular and so bright that they look painted, and the mist moves through them in the morning, turning the valley into a soft, silvery landscape. It is cool here, even when the plains below are baking, and the air has a faint smell of tea leaves.

The tea estates were set up in the late nineteenth century by British planters, who cleared forests and brought in labourers from Tamil Nadu to work the slopes, and the industry still shapes the town. A tea museum shows the old machinery, and the factories around the town can be visited. The hills around Munnar also contain Eravikulam National Park, home of the Nilgiri tahr, a rare mountain goat, and of Anamudi, at 2,695 metres the highest peak in South India. Every twelve years, the slopes around the town turn blue with the flowers of the neelakurinji, a plant that blooms only once in a dozen years, and the next flowering is expected around 2030.

The roads around Munnar are some of the best in Kerala, with winding bends through tea gardens, past waterfalls, lakes and viewpoints. The surface is generally good, though narrow in places, with steep drops and little barrier, and the weather can be wet and foggy, particularly in the monsoon from June to September. The best riding months are from October to March, when the days are clear and cool. Early mornings and late afternoons are the best times for light and for avoiding the heaviest traffic.

Munnar is a busy tourist town with about sixty-eight thousand people in the wider area, and it has fuel stations, shops, hotels and restaurants. The bazaar sells spices, tea, chocolate and local crafts, and there are plenty of places to eat, from simple Kerala meals to Chinese and Indian dishes. It gets crowded during holidays, so book accommodation early, and bring a warm jacket, since the evenings can be chilly.
